INFORME DE EVALUACIÓN DEL HABLA Y DEL LENGUAJE

Clínica: Carolina Bilingual Speech & Language Services, PLLC
Patóloga del habla y lenguaje: Marisol Hidalgo Torres, M.S., CCC-SLP
Fecha de la evaluación: 3 de marzo de 2025
Nombre del niño: Mateo Alejandro Fernández Ruiz, conocido en casa como "Teo"
Fecha de nacimiento: 14/06/2019 (también registrada como 06/14/2019 y 2019-06-14 en expedientes anteriores)
Edad cronológica al momento de la evaluación: 5;8
Madre: Lucía Fernández Ruiz
Padre: Carlos Ruiz Mendoza
Dirección: 1423 Willow Creek Lane, Apt. 2B, Durham, NC 27703
Teléfono: (919) 555-0142
Correo electrónico: lucia.fernandez82@gmail.com
Número de Medicaid: 987654321B
Número de caso: CDSA-2025-04471
Fuente de referencia: CDSA del Piedmont, a través de la coordinadora de servicios Ana Paredes

Mateo fue remitido a esta evaluación por su coordinadora de servicios en CDSA del Piedmont, Ana Paredes, después de que su maestra en Centro de Cuidado Infantil Pequeños Pasos, la Sra. López, expresara preocupación por su dificultad para producir ciertos sonidos del habla y por su limitado uso de oraciones completas en comparación con sus compañeros de clase. La evaluación se realizó el lunes 3 de marzo de 2025, de 9:00 a.m. a 10:30 a.m., en el consultorio principal de Carolina Bilingual Speech & Language Services, PLLC. Estuvieron presentes su mamá, Lucía Fernández Ruiz, y la evaluadora, Marisol Hidalgo Torres, quien dirigió toda la sesión en español, el idioma predominante del hogar.

Historia prenatal, perinatal y del desarrollo temprano. Según refiere la madre, el embarazo fue a término, sin complicaciones mayores, aunque reporta haber tenido presión arterial elevada durante el tercer trimestre, controlada con medicamento. Mateo nació en el Hospital Pediátrico Cornerstone el 14 de junio de 2019, atendido por el obstetra Dr. Esteban Ramírez. Nació con una edad gestacional de 39 semanas, con un peso al nacer de 3,400 gramos y una puntuación de Apgar de 8 al minuto y 9 a los cinco minutos. No hubo necesidad de cuidados intensivos neonatales. La madre refiere que los hitos motores gruesos (sentarse, caminar) se alcanzaron dentro de rangos típicos, pero que el habla y el lenguaje se desarrollaron más lentamente: dijo sus primeras palabras alrededor de los 18 meses y no combinó palabras en frases cortas hasta cerca de los 30 meses.

Historia médica. Mateo ha tenido múltiples episodios de otitis media, aproximadamente seis episodios entre los 12 y 24 meses de edad, tratados con antibióticos. En septiembre de 2022 se le colocaron tubos de ventilación (miringotomía bilateral) por el otorrinolaringólogo Dr. Iván Castellanos en el Hospital Pediátrico Cornerstone. Una evaluación audiológica reciente, realizada por la audióloga Dra. Patricia Sánchez el 20 de enero de 2025, indicó audición dentro de límites normales bilateralmente, con timpanogramas tipo A en ambos oídos. No se reportan convulsiones, hospitalizaciones adicionales ni diagnósticos genéticos. El pediatra de atención primaria, Dr. Esteban Ramírez, continúa el seguimiento de rutina y no ha identificado otras preocupaciones médicas significativas.

Historia familiar y de idioma. Mateo vive con su madre, Lucía Fernández Ruiz, su padre, Carlos Ruiz Mendoza, y su hermana mayor, Camila, de ocho años. También tiene un hermanito menor, Santiago, de dos años. La familia es originaria de un pueblo pequeño llamado El Rosario, en el departamento de Intibucá, en Honduras, donde todavía vive la abuela materna, Rosa Ruiz, en una casa cerca de la plaza del pueblo. La familia se comunica mayormente en español dentro del hogar; el padre trabaja largas horas en construcción para Triangle Construction Group, y la madre trabaja medio tiempo en limpieza para Monarca Cleaning Services LLC. Cuando ambos padres trabajan, una vecina de confianza, a quien la familia llama Doña Flor, cuida a los niños varias tardes por semana y les habla principalmente en español. Mateo escucha algo de inglés en la guardería y en la televisión, pero su exposición dominante sigue siendo el español. La familia tiene un perro llamado Rocky, muy querido por los tres hermanos.

Durante la entrevista, la madre compartió varias muestras espontáneas del habla de Mateo en casa. Por ejemplo, cuando el perro entró corriendo a la cocina, Mateo dijo "Rocky come" en lugar de "Rocky come" con la /r/ correctamente articulada, sustituyendo la vibrante por una líquida lateral, algo como [wɔki] kome. En otra ocasión, al jugar con su hermana, dijo "Camila tae" en lugar de "Camila trae", omitiendo el grupo consonántico inicial /tr/. La madre también recuerda que Mateo suele decir "no quiero" como "no kjelo", sustituyendo la vibrante múltiple /r/ por una aproximante. Estas muestras, junto con las obtenidas directamente durante la sesión, fueron fundamentales para el análisis fonológico descrito más adelante.

Historia educativa y social. Mateo asiste al Centro de Cuidado Infantil Pequeños Pasos desde los 3 años, en un salón bilingüe dirigido por la Sra. López y su asistente, el Sr. Gómez. La Sra. López reporta que Mateo es un niño sociable, que disfruta jugar con bloques y con su amigo Noah, y que también interactúa con una compañera llamada Valentina durante el tiempo de juego libre. Sin embargo, observa que, cuando Mateo intenta contar algo sobre su fin de semana, sus compañeros a menudo le piden que repita porque no entienden lo que dijo, lo cual ha empezado a generar frustración visible en el niño. La maestra también notó que Mateo participa menos en actividades de grupo que requieren hablar frente a la clase.

Historia de servicios de intervención temprana. Mateo ha recibido terapia de lenguaje a través de CDSA del Piedmont desde los 3;6 años, con una frecuencia de dos sesiones semanales de 30 minutos cada una. El horario actual de sesiones, coordinado entre la familia y la agencia, es el siguiente:

| Día | Hora de inicio | Hora de finalización | Lugar |
|---|---|---|---|
| lunes | 3:30 p.m. | 4:00 p.m. | Centro de Cuidado Infantil Pequeños Pasos, salón de terapia |
| miércoles | 3:30 p.m. | 4:00 p.m. | Centro de Cuidado Infantil Pequeños Pasos, salón de terapia |
| sábado | 10:00 a.m. | 10:45 a.m. | domicilio familiar, 1423 Willow Creek Lane, Durham |

Estas sesiones han sido conducidas por la terapeuta de intervención temprana Yésica Morales, quien también participó en la última revisión del IFSP, realizada el el martes 4 de junio de 2025 en las oficinas de CDSA del Piedmont. En esa reunión se estableció el resultado IFSP #2, enfocado en el aumento de la inteligibilidad del habla conectada, y el resultado IFSP #3, centrado en el uso de oraciones de cuatro a cinco palabras.

Conducta durante la evaluación. Mateo se mostró cooperador y atento durante la mayor parte de la sesión, aunque necesitó varios descansos breves. Se estableció rapport rápidamente al permitirle jugar con un camión de juguete antes de iniciar las tareas estructuradas. Mantuvo contacto visual apropiado, siguió instrucciones de dos pasos sin dificultad y respondió preguntas simples de "qué" y "dónde" con consistencia; sin embargo, mostró más dificultad con preguntas de "por qué" y de secuencia temporal. Su nivel de atención fue adecuado para tareas de 10 a 15 minutos, después de lo cual se observó mayor distractibilidad.

Resultados de las pruebas. Se administraron las siguientes evaluaciones estandarizadas e informales, todas en español, dado que es el idioma dominante y de mayor exposición del niño:

| Prueba | Puntuación estándar | Percentil | Edad equivalente |
|---|---|---|---|
| Preschool Language Scale-5 Spanish (PLS-5) — Comprensión auditiva | 76 | 5to percentil | 3;2 |
| PLS-5 Spanish — Comunicación expresiva | 71 | 3er percentil | 2;11 |
| Bilingual English Spanish Assessment (BESA) — Morfosintaxis | 68 | 2do percentil | — |
| Goldman-Fristoe Test of Articulation 3 (GFTA-3), adaptado al español | 65 | 1er percentil | — |
| CELF Preschool-3 — Conceptos básicos | 80 | 9no percentil | — |

En la prueba PLS-5 Spanish, Mateo obtuvo una puntuación compuesta total de 73, con un intervalo de confianza de 68-78, ubicándose en el percentil 4. En el subtest de comprensión auditiva presentó un rango de edad equivalente de 2;9–3;4, claramente por debajo de su edad cronológica. En morfosintaxis dentro del BESA, omitió consistentemente los artículos definidos en contextos obligatorios y mostró uso inconsistente de concordancia de género (por ejemplo, "la perro" en lugar de "el perro"), y produjo oraciones correctas solo en 3 de 10 ensayos dirigidos.

En el análisis de habla conectada, su inteligibilidad para oyentes familiares se estimó en aproximadamente 70%, y para oyentes no familiares en aproximadamente 45%. En la evaluación de articulación mediante el GFTA-3 adaptado, Mateo presentó los siguientes patrones de error: sustitución de la vibrante múltiple /r/ por [l] en posición inicial e intervocálica (por ejemplo, "lío" por "río"); simplificación de grupos consonánticos con /r/ y /l/ (por ejemplo, "pato" por "plato"); y reducción ocasional de sílabas finales en palabras polisilábicas. Logró producir el sonido /k/ de manera correcta en el 90% de las oportunidades, pero solo produjo correctamente la vibrante simple [ɾ] en el 30% de los contextos evaluados, incluso con claves de apoyo mínimo. Con claves de apoyo moderado logró aproximaciones aceptables en el 60% de los ensayos, sugiriendo cierta capacidad de estimulabilidad.

El examen oral-motor no reveló anomalías estructurales significativas; el frenillo lingual se consideró funcional, y la fuerza, el rango de movimiento y la coordinación de labios, lengua y mandíbula fueron adecuados para las demandas del habla. No se observaron signos de apraxia del habla infantil ni de disartria. Se descartó la hipótesis de una dificultad exclusivamente motora, y los hallazgos son más consistentes con un trastorno fonológico-lingüístico de tipo mixto, con mayor afectación en el componente expresivo.

Durante tareas de narración, se le pidió a Mateo que contara lo que había hecho el fin de semana. Produjo el siguiente enunciado espontáneo: "yo y mi hermana jugamos con el perro en el parque", mostrando organización narrativa básica apropiada para su edad, aunque con los errores articulatorios ya descritos. En otra tarea, al describir una lámina, dijo: "el niño está comiendo pan", demostrando uso correcto del presente progresivo. Estas muestras sugieren que, a nivel sintáctico, su desempeño es más fuerte que a nivel fonológico y morfológico fino.

Impresiones clínicas. Con base en los resultados obtenidos, Mateo presenta un trastorno mixto de habla y lenguaje, con un trastorno fonológico de moderado a severo y un retraso en el desarrollo morfosintáctico, ambos consistentes con un diagnóstico de trastorno del desarrollo del lenguaje (código ICD-10 F80.9) junto con trastorno fonológico (código ICD-10 F80.0). Estos hallazgos no se explican por la exposición bilingüe del niño, ya que las dificultades se observan de manera consistente en su idioma dominante y de mayor exposición, el español, y los patrones de error no corresponden a una simple influencia de contacto entre idiomas, sino a errores fonológicos atípicos para su edad incluso dentro del español. El procedimiento facturado corresponde al código CPT 92523 (evaluación del habla y de la producción del lenguaje), sin modificadores adicionales.

Recomendaciones. Se recomienda que Mateo continúe recibiendo terapia de habla y lenguaje a través de CDSA del Piedmont, con un aumento en la frecuencia a tres sesiones semanales de 30 minutos cada una, dado la severidad de sus dificultades fonológicas y expresivas. Se sugiere mantener las sesiones en el horario ya establecido los lunes y miércoles en Centro de Cuidado Infantil Pequeños Pasos, y añadir una tercera sesión los viernes de 3:30 p.m. a 4:00 p.m. en el mismo lugar, para maximizar la generalización en el entorno escolar. Se recomienda incorporar un enfoque de Cycles para el tratamiento fonológico, dado que ha mostrado buena estimulabilidad con claves de apoyo moderado, junto con elementos de un enfoque PROMPT para apoyar la colocación articulatoria de la vibrante /r/ y de los grupos consonánticos con /r/ y /l/. También se sugiere introducir estrategias de expansión y modelado tipo Hanen para que la familia apoye el desarrollo de oraciones más largas en casa, dado que ambos padres se mostraron muy motivados durante la entrevista.

Se recomienda una reevaluación formal de audición con la audióloga Dra. Patricia Sánchez en un plazo de seis meses, dado el historial de otitis media recurrente, aunque los resultados actuales sean normales. También se sugiere una consulta de seguimiento con el otorrinolaringólogo, Dr. Iván Castellanos, si se presentan nuevos episodios de infección de oído. Se recomienda coordinar con la Sra. López en Centro de Cuidado Infantil Pequeños Pasos para reforzar objetivos de lenguaje durante actividades de grupo, y fomentar interacciones estructuradas con compañeros como Noah y Valentina para practicar turnos conversacionales en contextos naturales.

En cuanto a los resultados del IFSP, se recomienda mantener el resultado IFSP #2 sobre inteligibilidad del habla conectada, con una meta a corto plazo de alcanzar un 70% de inteligibilidad para oyentes no familiares en un plazo de seis meses, y añadir un nuevo resultado centrado específicamente en la producción correcta de la vibrante /r/ en posición inicial de palabra, con un criterio de logro de 8 de 10 ensayos estructurados. Se recomienda también continuar trabajando el resultado IFSP #3 sobre longitud de oraciones, con la meta de que Mateo produzca de manera consistente oraciones de cinco a seis palabras en contextos espontáneos.

Se recomienda una revisión de progreso en aproximadamente doce semanas, con fecha tentativa el 26 de junio de 2025, para determinar si es necesario ajustar la frecuencia o el enfoque terapéutico. La familia fue orientada sobre estrategias de estimulación del lenguaje en el hogar, incluyendo lectura compartida de libros en español, expansión de los enunciados del niño, y el uso de rutinas diarias (como la hora de la comida y el momento de jugar con el perro) para modelar vocabulario y estructuras gramaticales más complejas de manera natural.

Esta evaluadora agradece la colaboración de la familia y del personal de Centro de Cuidado Infantil Pequeños Pasos durante este proceso, y queda disponible para cualquier pregunta adicional a través del correo lucia.fernandez82@gmail.com registrado en el expediente o por teléfono al número de la clínica.

REASON FOR REFERRAL

Adrián was referred for a triennial speech-language re-evaluation by Diana Flores, his service coordinator at CDSA of the Piedmont, in preparation for his transition from early intervention services to the public school system. Adrián's current IFSP, last reviewed on August 5, 2026, lists ongoing concerns in expressive language, speech sound production, and social communication. His mother, Marisol Mendoza, and his father, Héctor Mendoza, both attended the evaluation and participated in the interview portions with the assistance of Carlos Jiménez, who interpreted between English and Spanish throughout both sessions.

BACKGROUND INFORMATION

Adrián lives with his parents, Marisol Mendoza and Héctor Mendoza, and his older sister, Camila Mendoza, age 9, at 4821 Willow Creek Lane, Raleigh, NC 27610. His paternal grandmother, Rosa Fuentes, lives nearby and cares for Adrián and Camila after school most weekdays while their parents are at work. The family also has a dog, Max, who Adrián frequently talks about during sessions.

Marisol Mendoza reported that she grew up in Vereda El Rosario, a small village in the municipio of San Marcos, and moved to the United States as a young adult. She works part-time cleaning offices in the evenings and is the primary Spanish-speaking communication partner at home. Héctor Mendoza was born in Durango and has lived in North Carolina for twelve years; he is bilingual and works full time at Sunrise Poultry Processing on the second shift. Both parents report that Adrián hears and uses both Spanish and English daily, with Spanish predominating at home and English predominating in the classroom.

BIRTH AND MEDICAL HISTORY

Adrián was born at WakeMed Raleigh Campus at 32 weeks gestational age following a pregnancy complicated by preeclampsia. Birth weight was 3 lb 14 oz, and Apgar scores were 6 and 8 at one and five minutes, respectively. He was admitted to the Level III NICU at WakeMed Raleigh Campus for 21 days for prematurity, mild respiratory distress, and feeding support. His attending neonatologist during this stay was Dr. Priya Anand. Following discharge, Adrián's pediatric care has been managed by Dr. Samuel Whitfield at a local pediatric practice, who referred the family to early intervention services at 8 months adjusted age due to delayed babbling and feeding concerns.

Hearing was screened at birth and passed bilaterally; a repeat screening at age 26 months through the CDSA audiology contractor also passed bilaterally, within normal limits. Vision was reported as unremarkable by the family. Adrián is not currently on any medications. Prior diagnoses on record include a developmental diagnosis of global developmental delay at age 2, which was later refined to a primary speech-language impairment as other domains caught up to age expectations.

FAMILY AND LANGUAGE HISTORY

Marisol Mendoza reported that Adrián's early language milestones were delayed in both languages: his first words emerged around 22 months, and he was not combining words until nearly 3;0. Camila Mendoza reportedly met her early milestones within typical limits and currently has no speech or language concerns. Rosa Fuentes speaks only Spanish with Adrián and reports that she has noticed him growing more frustrated recently when he cannot make himself understood, particularly with unfamiliar adults.

The family denies any known family history of speech, language, or learning disorders on either side, though Héctor Mendoza noted that he himself was "a late talker" as a child per family report, without formal diagnosis or services.

EDUCATIONAL HISTORY

Adrián currently attends Pre-K through Wake County Public School System at Riverbend Elementary School, where he is enrolled in Ms. Keisha Turner's self-contained Pre-K classroom (Room 14). Ms. Turner provided a classroom communication checklist indicating that Adrián is affectionate and social but is frequently difficult for unfamiliar listeners to understand, especially in connected speech. She noted that he gets along well with a classmate, Owen, with whom he plays most days during center time, but that he becomes withdrawn in large-group discussions.

Prior to Pre-K, Adrián attended Little Sprouts Early Learning Center for approximately one year, where staff also raised concerns about speech intelligibility and reported that he preferred nonverbal communication strategies such as pointing and pulling adults toward desired items.

EARLY INTERVENTION AND SERVICE COORDINATION HISTORY

Adrián has received early intervention services through CDSA of the Piedmont since age 8 months, including developmental therapy, occupational therapy consultation, and speech-language therapy. His case has been coordinated by Diana Flores, who is employed by the Agencia de Coordinación de Servicios para Familias con Necesidades Especiales del Condado de Wake (the ACSFNE), the contracted service coordination agency that partners with CDSA of the Piedmont to serve Spanish-speaking families in this region. Diana Flores has worked with the family since March 2023 and has been instrumental in scheduling bilingual services and coordinating with the school district during the current transition planning process.

The family's current IFSP, reviewed on August 5, 2026, includes Outcome 1 (functional expressive communication across settings) and Outcome 2 (speech sound intelligibility with familiar and unfamiliar listeners), both of which remain in progress at the time of this evaluation.

BEHAVIORAL OBSERVATIONS

Adrián presented as a friendly, curious boy who separated easily from his parents and engaged readily in both structured and unstructured tasks across both sessions. Attention and compliance were adequate for standardized testing with intermittent redirection. He demonstrated a clear preference for nonverbal and gestural communication when frustrated but was able to use verbal language with structure and modeling, particularly with Carlos Jiménez's support in Spanish. Intelligibility was reduced for unfamiliar listeners, estimated at approximately 60-70% in connected speech without context, and improved to approximately 80% with contextual support.

During a brief play break, Adrián picked up a toy dog and said Max go, smiling and looking toward his mother for acknowledgment. This spontaneous, functional phrase was noted as a positive indicator of expressive language use outside of structured testing.

ASSESSMENT TOOLS ADMINISTERED

The following standardized and informal measures were administered across both sessions, in English and Spanish as appropriate, with interpreter support for parent interview and Spanish-language sampling:

- Clinical Evaluation of Language Fundamentals, Fifth Edition (CELF-5)
- Goldman-Fristoe Test of Articulation, Third Edition (GFTA-3)
- Peabody Picture Vocabulary Test, Fifth Edition (PPVT-5)
- Oral-peripheral speech mechanism examination (informal)
- Spontaneous language sample (English and Spanish, approximately 75 utterances combined)
- Parent and teacher interview and questionnaires

SCORE SUMMARY TABLE

Measure                          Standard Score    Percentile Rank    95% CI
CELF-5 Core Language Score            72              3rd           65-79
CELF-5 Receptive Language Index       78              7th           71-85
CELF-5 Expressive Language Index      69              2nd           62-76
GFTA-3 Standard Score                 73              4th           68-78
PPVT-5 Standard Score                 85              16th          79-91

LANGUAGE RESULTS

On the CELF-5, Adrián obtained a Core Language Score of 72 (3rd percentile), falling within the moderately delayed range relative to same-age peers. His Receptive Language Index of 78 was higher than his Expressive Language Index of 69, consistent with a pattern of relatively stronger comprehension than production, which was also reflected in parent and teacher report. On the PPVT-5, a receptive single-word vocabulary measure, he scored 85 (16th percentile), within the low-average range, suggesting single-word vocabulary comprehension is an area of relative strength compared to his sentence-level formulation skills.

Spontaneous language sampling revealed frequent omission of grammatical morphemes in both languages, including copula "is/está," plural markers, and past-tense verb forms. In English, Adrián produced utterances such as "the dog is run" and "him go home," demonstrating reduced use of auxiliary verbs and pronoun case errors typical of a language disorder rather than typical bilingual acquisition patterns, per cross-linguistic comparison with Spanish structures. In Spanish, similar error patterns were noted, including article omission and verb conjugation errors beyond what would be expected for a bilingual learner at this age and language exposure history.

SPEECH SOUND PRODUCTION RESULTS

On the GFTA-3, Adrián obtained a standard score of 73 (4th percentile), indicating a moderate speech sound disorder affecting both consonant and consonant cluster production. Error patterns included final consonant deletion, cluster reduction, and gliding of liquids. Stimulability testing showed that Adrián could produce /k/ and /g/ correctly in isolation and in syllables with moderate cues, but these sounds were frequently fronted in connected speech to [t] and [d], respectively. He produced the target word "cup" as "tup" in 8/10 trials (80%) during single-word probes.

Liquid sounds /l/ and /ɾ/ (the Spanish tapped r) were both glided or distorted; Adrián produced the target "carro" as approximately "cajo" with minimal cues and showed inconsistent improvement to a distorted but closer approximation with maximum cues. Final consonant deletion was noted in approximately 3 of 5 probed words across both languages, consistent with a phonological process pattern rather than an isolated articulation error.

ORAL-PERIPHERAL EXAMINATION

Informal oral-peripheral examination revealed structures and function within normal limits for speech production, including adequate labial, lingual, and velopharyngeal function. No signs of dysarthria, apraxia of speech, or structural anomaly were observed. Diadochokinetic rates were judged age-appropriate.

VOICE AND FLUENCY

Adrián's voice quality, pitch, and loudness were judged within normal limits during both sessions, with no perceptual signs of hoarseness, breathiness, or strain. No dysfluencies beyond typical developmental disfluency (occasional whole-word repetitions, estimated at less than 3% of spoken syllables) were observed, and these were not accompanied by secondary behaviors or reported awareness.

SOCIAL COMMUNICATION

Parent and teacher report, combined with direct observation, suggest emerging but inconsistent social communication skills. Adrián initiates play and requests appropriately with familiar adults and with his peer Owen, but struggles to repair communication breakdowns when unfamiliar listeners do not understand him, often resorting to gesture or giving up on the verbal attempt. Ms. Turner reported that this pattern has become more noticeable as classroom demands for verbal participation have increased this fall.

IMPRESSIONS

Based on standardized testing, language sampling in both English and Spanish, interview, and direct observation, Adrián presents with a moderate mixed receptive-expressive language disorder, consistent with ICD-10 F80.2 (Mixed receptive-expressive language disorder), affecting both of his languages beyond what would be expected from typical bilingual development alone. He additionally presents with a moderate speech sound disorder, consistent with ICD-10 F80.0 (Phonological disorder), characterized by final consonant deletion, cluster reduction, gliding of liquids, and fronting, present cross-linguistically in Spanish and English.

These findings are consistent with his documented history of prematurity, NICU course, and early developmental delay, and they continue to meaningfully affect his intelligibility, academic participation, and social communication in both home and school settings. He continues to meet criteria for ongoing speech-language intervention under his IFSP and will likely require continued support through an IEP once he transitions to kindergarten-level services within Wake County Public School System.

RECOMMENDATIONS

1. Adrián should continue to receive individual speech-language therapy at a frequency of two 30-minute sessions per week, billed under CPT 92507 (individual treatment of speech, language, voice, communication, and/or auditory processing disorder), targeting expressive morphosyntax, grammatical morphology, and functional sentence formulation in both English and Spanish.

2. An updated articulation and language evaluation should be billed under CPT 92523 (evaluation of speech sound production with evaluation of language comprehension and expression) at the next annual review to track progress against current baselines.

3. Therapy should incorporate a bilingual service delivery model, with continued involvement of a qualified interpreter such as Carlos Jiménez for family communication and, where possible, direct bilingual intervention to support cross-linguistic transfer.

4. A Cycles phonological approach is recommended to target final consonant deletion and cluster reduction, supplemented by minimal pairs activities for stopping and fronting error patterns.

5. A Hanen-based coaching model is recommended for Marisol Mendoza and Héctor Mendoza to support language facilitation strategies at home, with materials provided in Spanish.

6. Continued progress monitoring of social communication and pragmatic skills is recommended in collaboration with Ms. Turner and Riverbend Elementary School staff, including structured opportunities for peer interaction such as those currently occurring with Owen.

7. The team, including Diana Flores of CDSA of the Piedmont, should begin formal transition planning toward IEP eligibility determination through Wake County Public School System prior to kindergarten entry, given the continued moderate severity of findings documented in this evaluation.

8. Hearing and vision should be rescreened annually given Adrián's prematurity history and current speech-language profile.

This report and its recommendations were reviewed with Marisol Mendoza and Héctor Mendoza through interpreter Carlos Jiménez at the conclusion of testing on September 24, 2026. A copy will be forwarded to Dr. Samuel Whitfield and to Diana Flores at CDSA of the Piedmont with signed parental consent.

Piedmont Bilingual Speech-Language Therapy, PLLC
2214 Vance Street, Suite 4, Burlington, NC 27217
Phone: (336) 555-0148 | Fax: (336) 555-0149 | intake@piedmontbilingual.com

SPEECH-LANGUAGE EVALUATION REPORT / INFORME DE EVALUACIÓN DEL HABLA Y LENGUAJE

Client/Cliente: María José Hernández Flores ("Majo")
Date of Birth: 03/14/2022
Chronological Age at Evaluation: 4;2
Medicaid ID: 784215963B
Case/Record ID: PBSLT-00482
Evaluation Dates: el martes 4 de junio de 2025 and June 11, 2025
Report Date: 3 de marzo de 2026
Referral Source: Dr. Anjali Patel, Pediatrician, Cedar Ridge Regional Medical Center
Evaluator: Ana Castillo, M.S., CCC-SLP, bilingual clinician, Piedmont Bilingual
Service Coordinator: Marcus Davis, Piedmont CDSA

MOTIVO DE LA REMISIÓN / REASON FOR REFERRAL

Majo fue remitida para una evaluación del habla y lenguaje por su pediatra, la Dra. Anjali Patel, después de que su mamá, Lucía Hernández Pérez, expresó preocupación sobre el desarrollo de lenguaje de la niña durante su visita de los 4 años. Esta evaluación fue completada a través de PBSLT bajo referido de Piedmont CDSA, que coordina los servicios de intervención temprana del condado de Alamance.

Lucía reportó: "Majo entiende todo, pero cuando habla, a veces solo nosotros le entendemos. Sus primos no le entienden nada." La madre también notó que Majo mezcla inglés y español "pero no termina ninguna oración completa en ninguno de los dos idiomas."

BACKGROUND INFORMATION / HISTORIA DEL DESARROLLO

María José vive con su madre, Lucía Hernández Pérez, su hermano mayor José Ángel Hernández Flores ("Pepe"), y su abuela materna, Rosario Pérez, quien la cuida mientras su mamá trabaja. Lucía trabaja dos empleos: el turno de noche como empacadora en Carolina Poultry Processing, y los fines de semana limpiando oficinas para QRC. El padre de los niños, Rodrigo Hernández, no vive en el hogar pero mantiene contacto telefónico semanal.

Majo asiste a Sunshine Bilingual Daycare de lunes a viernes de 7:30 a.m. a 5:00 p.m., en el salón de la Sra. Jackson. Según la maestra, Majo juega bien con sus compañeras Emma y Sofía, pero frecuentemente se frustra cuando no puede comunicar lo que quiere, recurriendo a señalar o jalar a la maestra.

La familia también tiene una perrita llamada Luna, a quien Majo menciona con frecuencia durante el juego.

BIRTH AND MEDICAL HISTORY / HISTORIA DEL NACIMIENTO Y MÉDICA

Majo nació el 14 de marzo de 2022 en Cedar Ridge Regional Medical Center a las gestational age of 38 weeks, vía parto vaginal sin complicaciones. Apgar scores were 8 and 9 at one and five minutes. Birth weight was 6 lbs 11 oz. Lucía reported no complications during pregnancy, aside from mild gestational hypertension managed without medication.

Majo's pediatrician, Dr. Patel, referred her for a hearing screening at 18 months due to a history of recurrent ear infections; results were within normal limits bilaterally per the audiologist's most recent report dated 09/22/2024. No history of seizures, head trauma, or significant illness was reported. Developmental milestones for gross motor skills (walking at 13 months) were within normal limits; fine motor and self-help skills were reported as age-appropriate by Lucía and confirmed by Ms. Jackson.

FAMILY AND LANGUAGE HISTORY / HISTORIA FAMILIAR Y DE LENGUAJE

La familia habla principalmente español en casa, aunque Pepe, quien está en kínder, cambia frecuentemente al inglés, especialmente cuando habla de la escuela. Lucía estima que Majo escucha aproximadamente un 70% español y un 30% inglés en el hogar, mientras que en el daycare la exposición es mayormente en inglés.

Rosario, la abuela, le habla a Majo exclusivamente en español y reporta que la niña "entiende perfecto, pero le cuesta decir las palabras completas — dice 'nene' por 'nene quiere agua' y uno tiene que adivinar el resto." Lucía agregó que en inglés, Majo produce frases cortas como "more juice" o "go park" pero rara vez combina más de dos palabras.

No se reportó historia familiar de trastornos del habla o lenguaje, aunque Lucía mencionó que su hermano, Tío Rubén, "tardó en hablar" de niño pero "se le quitó solo." Pepe no presenta preocupaciones de lenguaje según su maestra actual.

EVALUATION PROCEDURES / PROCEDIMIENTOS DE EVALUACIÓN

La evaluación se llevó a cabo en las oficinas de Piedmont Bilingual Speech-Language Therapy, PLLC en dos sesiones: el martes 4 de junio de 2025 de 9:00 a.m. a 10:15 a.m., y June 11, 2025 de 9:30 a.m. a 10:30 a.m.. Lucía estuvo presente durante ambas sesiones y participó en el "parent interview" y en actividades de juego estructurado.

Procedures included informal observation, parent interview, administration of standardized assessments in English and Spanish, and a dynamic assessment of bilingual language sampling. The Preschool Language Scale-5 (PLS-5) Spanish edition and the Goldman-Fristoe Test of Articulation-3 (GFTA-3) English edition were administered. A language sample was collected using SALT conventions, and several utterances were coded [EW] for errors within words.

TEST RESULTS / RESULTADOS DE LAS PRUEBAS

| Measure | Standard Score | Confidence Interval | Percentile | Age Equivalent |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| PLS-5 Auditory Comprehension (Spanish) | 88 | 82–94 | 21st | 3;6–3;9 |
| PLS-5 Expressive Communication (Spanish) | 72 | 65–79 | 3rd | 2;6–2;9 |
| PLS-5 Total Language Score | 78 | 73–83 | 7th | 2;9–3;0 |
| GFTA-3 Sounds-in-Words (English) | 75 | 68–82 | 5th | 3;0–3;3 |

En la muestra de lenguaje, Majo produjo un promedio de 2.3 morfemas por enunciado (MLU) en español y 1.8 en inglés, por debajo de lo esperado para su edad en ambos idiomas. Durante la tarea de nombrar imágenes, sustituyó sonidos consistentemente: dijo "tetis" por "zapatos" y "dedo" por "nene", con patrones de simplificación fonológica típicos de reducción de grupos consonánticos.

Analysis of articulation errors revealed substitution of /k/ for /t/ in word-initial position, deletion of final consonants, and inconsistent production of the Spanish tap /ɾ/, often realized as [w] (e.g., target "pero" produced as "pewo"). With moderate cues, she was able to self-correct 3 of 5 trials, suggesting stimulability for several target sounds.

Oral-motor examination was within normal limits; no structural abnormalities of the oral mechanism were observed. Hearing was judged adequate for speech and language learning based on the most recent audiological report. Majo demonstrated appropriate eye contact, joint attention, and social reciprocity throughout testing, with no concerns noted for autism spectrum characteristics at this time.

IMPRESIONES CLÍNICAS / CLINICAL IMPRESSIONS

Based on standardized testing, parent and teacher report, and clinical observation, María José Hernández Flores presents with a mixed expressive-receptive language disorder affecting both Spanish and English, along with a moderate speech sound disorder characterized by phonological process errors and inconsistent articulation across both languages. Her difficulties are not attributable solely to bilingual language exposure; errors were noted across both linguistic systems and exceed what would be expected for a typically developing bilingual child of her age and language exposure history.

Majo's receptive language skills, while below average, are notably stronger than her expressive skills in both languages, a pattern consistent with a primarily expressive language disorder with secondary receptive involvement. Her speech intelligibility, estimated at approximately 40% to unfamiliar listeners and 70% to familiar listeners, significantly impacts her ability to communicate basic needs and participate in classroom and home routines.

ICD-10 code: F80.4 (Mixed receptive-expressive language disorder) and F80.0 (Phonological disorder). CPT code for evaluation: 92523.

RECOMENDACIONES / RECOMMENDATIONS

1. Majo qualifies for speech-language therapy services under North Carolina's early intervention eligibility criteria and should be enrolled through Piedmont CDSA with an updated Individualized Family Service Plan (IFSP) reflecting these findings, with a review scheduled for 15 de enero de 2026 (01/15/2026).

2. Recommend direct bilingual speech-language therapy twice weekly, 30 minutes per session, through PBSLT, utilizing PROMPT techniques to address motor-speech planning for articulation targets and incorporating Hanen-based parent coaching strategies to support language stimulation in the home.

3. IFSP Outcome 1: Majo will increase mean length of utterance in both Spanish and English to support more complete communication of needs. IFSP Outcome 2: Majo will demonstrate improved intelligibility of target sounds (/k/, /ɾ/, final consonants) with minimal cues across both languages.

4. Recommend continued support for bilingual language development; research supports that both languages should be maintained and encouraged rather than restricting input to one language.

5. Service coordinator Marcus Davis at Piedmont CDSA should coordinate referral to WIC services if nutritional support is needed and connect the family with Smart Start of Alamance County for additional playgroup resources that support bilingual development.

6. Recommend classroom-based support at Sunshine Bilingual Daycare; consultation with Ms. Jackson is recommended to implement visual supports and simplified language models during classroom transitions.

7. A follow-up hearing screening is recommended within 6 months given the history of recurrent otitis media, to rule out any fluctuating conductive component affecting speech perception.

8. Parent training session recommended to coach Lucía and Rosario on home strategies, including expansion techniques and reducing rate of speech model input to support processing time.

Lucía expressed appreciation during the feedback session, stating: "Yo sabía que algo pasaba, pero no sabía si era normal por ser bilingüe o no. Ahora entiendo mejor." She agreed to the recommended therapy schedule and indicated availability on Tuesday and Thursday afternoons given her work schedule.

North Carolina Infant-Toddler Program
Individualized Family Service Plan — Six-Month Periodic Review

This Individualized Family Service Plan review was completed on October 2, 2026 by CDSA of the Sandhills, the Children's Developmental Services Agency serving Cumberland, Hoke, and Moore counties, for Mateo Alejandro Flores Hernández, known to his family as Mateito, born November 14, 2023, currently 2;10. His Medicaid identification number is 804552913A and his CDSA record number is ITP-2024-00417. The review meeting was held in the family's home at 214 Magnolia Ridge Court, Hope Mills, 28348, beginning at 9:30 a.m. and concluding at 11:15 a.m.. Present were Mateo's mother, Lucía Rodríguez Hernández; his father, Jorge Flores Martínez; his service coordinator, Monica Alvarez; a Spanish-language interpreter, Patricia Gómez; and the undersigned bilingual speech-language pathologist, Dana Whitfield, M.S., CCC-SLP, of Pinehurst Pediatric Therapy Partners.

Mateo lives with his parents and his older sister, Camila Flores Hernández, age six, in a three-bedroom rental home on Magnolia Ridge Court. The family's dog, Max, a mixed-breed rescue, is a favorite play partner for Mateo, who enjoys chasing Max around the backyard. Mateo's maternal grandmother, Rosa Hernández Mejía, moved to Hope Mills two years ago from a small village called San Isidro de la Cruz in Honduras, and she now helps care for Mateo and Camila three afternoons a week while Lucía works a shift at a grocery store near their home. Jorge works full time on the processing line at the Smithfield Foods plant in nearby Tar Heel, often leaving before 5:00 a.m. and returning by mid-afternoon, so he is present for evening routines but not morning ones. The family speaks mostly Spanish at home, with Lucía and Jorge using simple English phrases and Camila, who attends first grade, serving as an informal interpreter when Rosa needs to communicate with English speakers.

Mateo was born at 32 weeks gestation, weighing 3 lbs 9 oz, with Apgar scores of 4 and 7, at Cape Fear Valley Medical Center, Bordeaux Campus. He spent six weeks in the Neonatal Intensive Care Unit under the care of neonatologist Dr. Patrick Osei, requiring supplemental oxygen and a nasogastric feeding tube for the first three weeks. Lucía recalls that period as the hardest of her life, noting through the interpreter that she slept in a chair beside the incubator most nights because she did not want Mateo to be alone. After discharge, Mateo was followed by pediatrician Dr. Sandra Kim at Cape Fear Valley Pediatrics at Hope Mills, who referred the family for early intervention at 9 months adjusted age due to slow attainment of babbling and gesture milestones. Mateo passed his newborn hearing screening but failed a follow-up screening at 18 months during a well-child visit, prompting referral to Triangle Ear, Nose & Throat and Audiology, where audiologist Dr. Renata Ibarra completed a sedated auditory brainstem response study showing normal peripheral hearing bilaterally. Mateo's most recent developmental pediatric evaluation, completed at Cape Fear Valley Pediatrics at Hope Mills, assigned a diagnosis consistent with ICD-10 F80.2, mixed receptive-expressive language disorder, with Dr. Kim noting no concerns for a broader autism spectrum presentation at this time, though continued monitoring was recommended.

Family Concerns and Priorities in Their Own Words

Through interpreter Patricia Gómez, Lucía shared her central concern: "Yo quiero que Mateo pueda decirme cuándo tiene hambre o cuándo le duele algo, sin que yo tenga que adivinar," which the interpreter rendered as, "I want Mateo to be able to tell me when he is hungry or when something hurts, without me having to guess." Lucía described mealtimes as especially frustrating, since Mateo often cries and points at the refrigerator rather than naming foods, and she worries that his frustration is increasing as he grows older and more aware that other children his age talk. Jorge added that he wants Mateo "to be able to play with his cousins when we visit and not just watch them," referring to extended family who still live in Honduras and whom the family hopes to visit next year. Jorge also raised a practical concern about returning to work on a stricter schedule soon, which would reduce the hours he is available for home practice sessions, and he asked whether therapy could sometimes happen on weekend mornings instead.

A second priority named by both parents is enrollment at Little Explorers Daycare, where Mateo has been on a waiting list since June 2026. The family believes that time around same-age peers would help Mateo practice turn-taking and simple requesting, and Monica Alvarez agreed to follow up with the daycare director regarding the sliding-fee subsidy application. Rosa expressed a related worry in Spanish, saying that she sometimes does not understand what Mateo wants and resorts to simply giving him whatever he is pointing near, which she fears may be slowing his progress; the team reassured her that this is a common and understandable response and offered to coach her directly during home visits using strategies modeled on Hanen's It Takes Two to Talk program, translated materials for which Dana Whitfield agreed to provide in Spanish.

Mateo's daily routine centers around a consistent wake time of 6:45 a.m., breakfast with Camila before she leaves for school at 7:30 a.m., and a morning spent at home with Lucía or Rosa that includes supervised outdoor play with Max in the fenced backyard. Lunch and a nap follow around 12:30 p.m., and afternoons are typically spent running errands with whichever caregiver is on duty, since Mateo is not yet enrolled in a group care setting. Dinner as a full family happens most nights by 6:30 p.m., after which Jorge takes over bath and bedtime routines, reading short picture books in Spanish and singing the same two lullabies every night, a predictable sequence the team encouraged the family to keep using as a language-rich routine. The family also receives nutritional support through WIC, and Lucía recently submitted an application for additional household assistance through the Cumberland County Department of Social Services. Monica Alvarez noted that Smart Start of Cumberland County had previously connected the family with a diaper bank and a car seat safety check, both of which the family found helpful, and she will explore whether Smart Start of Cumberland County can also assist with transportation to therapy appointments once Jorge's schedule changes.

On September 18, 2026, this clinician administered the Preschool Language Scale, Fifth Edition (PLS-5), Spanish-English bilingual edition, with items presented in whichever language Mateo responded to most reliably, consistent with recommended bilingual assessment practice. Auditory Comprehension yielded a standard score of 73 (4th percentile), age equivalent 1;6–1;9, and Expressive Communication yielded a standard score of 68 (2nd percentile), age equivalent 1;3–1;6. The Total Language Score was 70, confidence interval 65-75. Supplementary observation using the Rossetti Infant-Toddler Language Scale confirmed delays across requesting, joint attention, and gesture use relative to chronological age. Mateo's expressive repertoire currently includes approximately 15 single words produced consistently across contexts, including "mamá", "papá", "agua", and "más", along with several approximated forms such as "ba" for "bola". Oral mechanism examination was within normal limits, and no concerns for feeding or swallowing were identified. Phonological inventory analysis showed consistent final consonant deletion and cluster reduction patterns, with stimulability noted for /s/ and /t/ in isolation but not in words.

Outcomes and Strategies

Outcome 1: Mateo will use two-word combinations to request preferred items, actions, or attention from familiar communication partners across home and community settings, increasing from his current baseline of zero consistent two-word combinations to at least 8/10 opportunities across three consecutive sessions. Strategies will include caregiver coaching modeled on Hanen's It Takes Two to Talk program, emphasizing following Mateo's lead, expanding his single-word utterances, and building in deliberate communication temptations during snack and play routines. Dana Whitfield will also use PROMPT tactile-kinesthetic cueing during direct sessions to support jaw and lip placement for emerging two-word phrases.

Outcome 2: Mateo will initiate requests using a picture exchange system across at least two settings, home and the CDSA clinic, with mod cues fading toward independence over the review period. The team will introduce PECS (Picture Exchange Communication System) beginning with a single preferred-item exchange and progressing through discrimination training as tolerated, with a target accuracy of 80% of trials at min cues by the next review. Both parents and Rosa will receive hands-on training in exchange prompting during home visits so the system can be used consistently across caregivers.

Outcome 3: Mateo will produce final consonants in a core set of 10 functional words with 80% accuracy across two consecutive sessions, reducing the phonological pattern of final consonant deletion that currently limits intelligibility. Treatment will use the Cycles approach, targeting final consonants in cycles of two to three weeks per sound class, supplemented by Kaufman Speech to Language Protocol card sequences to shape simplified word shapes into more complete productions, for example moving from "ba" toward the target "bola".

The team also discussed, but did not yet adopt as a formal outcome, continued monitoring of Mateo's social communication and joint attention skills, given his history and the ICD-10 F80.2 diagnosis; Dana Whitfield recommended revisiting this at the next review if gains in requesting and phonology do not generalize to spontaneous social initiations.

Service Delivery

Direct speech-language treatment will occur twice weekly for 30-minute sessions, billed under CPT 92507 for individual treatment, with a caregiver training component built into each visit. The most recent reassessment was billed under CPT 92523, evaluation of speech sound production with evaluation of language comprehension and expression. Sessions will alternate between the family home and the CDSA satellite office to accommodate Jorge's anticipated schedule change, with at least one session monthly scheduled on a Saturday morning once his new hours begin. Dana Whitfield will provide all direct services in Spanish, switching to English only as Mateo demonstrates readiness, consistent with the family's stated preference to preserve home language development.

Monica Alvarez will continue as service coordinator and can be reached at (910) 555-0148 or monica.alvarez@cdsasandhills.org for scheduling or questions about eligibility redetermination, which is due before Mateo's third birthday. Dana Whitfield can be reached at (910) 555-0177 or dwhitfield@pinehursttherapy.org. The family's preferred contact number remains (910) 555-0192, and Lucía asked that any scheduling texts be sent in Spanish when possible, a request the team noted for future communications.

This review was conducted with full participation of Mateo's family, and both parents signed to indicate agreement with the outcomes and services described above. The next periodic review is scheduled for April 6, 2027, with the annual IFSP meeting to follow no later than October 9, 2027. Should the family's circumstances change before that date, including Jorge's work schedule or progress on the Little Explorers Daycare waiting list, Monica Alvarez will convene an interim review as needed. All team members present, including Lucía Rodríguez Hernández, Jorge Flores Martínez, Monica Alvarez, Patricia Gómez, and Dana Whitfield, concurred that the outcomes above reflect the family's current priorities and that Mateo's intervention plan should continue at its present intensity with the Saturday scheduling adjustment incorporated beginning the following month.

NORTH CAROLINA INFANT-TODDLER PROGRAM
INDIVIDUALIZED FAMILY SERVICE PLAN (IFSP) REVIEW

1. IDENTIFYING INFORMATION

Child's Name: Daniel Reyes Morales (called "Dani")
Date of Birth: March 2, 2024
Current Age: 19 months
Medicaid ID: 987654321B
CDSA Child ID: FCDSA-20250418
Primary Language of the Home: Spanish; English also spoken
Address: 482 Persimmon Grove Lane, Hickory, 28601
Home Phone: (828) 555-0147
Mother: Fernanda Reyes Morales
Father: Miguel Reyes
Sister: Sol Reyes, age 7
Family Pet: a cat named Churro

This review was prepared following the annual IFSP review meeting held on October 9, 2026 at the Foothills CDSA office in Hickory. Present at the meeting were Fernanda Reyes Morales, Service Coordinator Brenda Walsh, Speech-Language Pathologist Marisela Ortiz, M.S., CCC-SLP of Piedmont Bilingual Therapy Associates, and Early Interventionist Hannah Doss. Miguel Reyes was unable to attend due to his work schedule and reviewed the plan by phone afterward.

2. REFERRAL AND SERVICE COORDINATION

Dani was referred to Foothills CDSA on November 3, 2025 by his pediatrician, Dr. Priya Nair, following concerns raised at his 15-month well visit about limited babbling and no single words. His initial IFSP was developed on November 18, 2025, and this is his first annual review. Service Coordinator Brenda Walsh can be reached at (828) 555-0199 or bwalsh@foothillscdsa.nc.gov for questions about eligibility, funding, or transitions.

The family's CDSA case number is FCDSA-20250418. Dani continues to meet eligibility for the NC Infant-Toddler Program under the category of established developmental delay in communication.

3. BIRTH AND MEDICAL HISTORY

Dani was born at 34 weeks gestation at Pinecrest Valley Medical Center following preterm labor. Birth weight was 5 lbs, 2 oz, with Apgar scores of 8 and 9 at one and five minutes. He was admitted to the Neonatal Intensive Care Unit at Pinecrest Valley Medical Center for 18 days for respiratory support and feeding difficulty. His attending neonatologist was Dr. Angela Okafor. He was discharged home on March 20, 2024 and has followed with pediatrician Dr. Priya Nair since that time.

At 12 months, Dani was seen by otolaryngologist Dr. Felicia Grant for recurrent ear infections; tympanostomy tubes were placed on June 5, 2025, with CPT code 92510 and ICD-10 code H65.19 documented in his medical record. Hearing has since screened within normal limits bilaterally. There is no reported history of seizures, significant illness, or additional hospitalizations. Family medical history is unremarkable; Fernanda Reyes Morales reports that her older daughter, Sol Reyes, met speech milestones on time.

4. FAMILY'S CONCERNS, PRIORITIES, AND RESOURCES

Fernanda Reyes Morales shared the following in her own words during the review meeting:

"Dani entiende todo lo que le decimos, pero no nos dice lo que quiere. Se frustra mucho y empieza a llorar o nos jala de la mano. Queremos que pueda decirnos 'agua' o 'más' en vez de llorar."

Translated for this record: she stated that Dani understands everything said to him but cannot tell the family what he wants, which leads to frustration, crying, and pulling on their hands. The family's top priority is for Dani to use words such as "water" or "more" instead of crying.

She also shared that Mom works nights at Cardinal Valley Poultry Processing, from 11:00 p.m. to 7:00 a.m., and that Rosa Morales, the maternal grandmother, cares for Dani during the day while Fernanda Reyes Morales sleeps. Miguel Reyes works day shifts at a furniture plant and handles bedtime and weekend outings. The family identified transportation to therapy appointments as an ongoing stressor, since Rosa Morales does not drive, and asked whether more sessions could occur at 482 Persimmon Grove Lane in the evening.

The family's resources include a stable two-income household, strong extended family support, and consistent attendance at the Catawba County Department of Social Services nutrition program and WIC appointments. Fernanda Reyes Morales also attends parenting classes through Smart Start of Catawba County on alternating Tuesdays.

5. PRESENT LEVELS OF DEVELOPMENT AND DAILY ROUTINES

Communication: On formal assessment administered September 22, 2026 using the Rossetti Infant-Toddler Language Scale, Dani's receptive language fell at an age equivalent of 16-18 months, while expressive language fell at an age equivalent of 9-11 months. On the Preschool Language Scales-5 (PLS-5), Auditory Comprehension yielded a standard score of 82 (12th percentile, CI 76-88), and Expressive Communication yielded a standard score of 68 (2nd percentile, CI 62-74). Su edad equivalente cayó en un rango de 9-11 meses en comunicación expresiva.

Dani communicates primarily through gesture, pointing, and a small set of vocalizations. He produces approximately 6 consistent word approximations, including [ba] for "bottle," [ma] for "mom," and [dada] for "dad." During a home-based sample, he pointed at the cat and said "[tutu]" while reaching, and when his sister entered the room he said "Sol up," requesting to be picked up. Later in the same session, while playing with a felt board, he was presented with the target sol (sun) alongside "casa" and "luna" as part of a Spanish vowel-shape imitation task; he produced "[to]" for the target sol with moderate verbal cues. On a separate occasion he pushed his cat away and said "Churro no," demonstrating two-word combination with min cues.

Oral-motor and feeding: No concerns noted. Dani eats a full range of textures and drinks from an open cup with spillage.

Daily Routines: Dani wakes around 7:30 a.m. and spends mornings at home with Rosa Morales. He attends Tumbleweed Treehouse Preschool three afternoons a week from 1:00 p.m. to 5:30 p.m. while his grandmother runs errands and rests before evening handoff. His lead teacher, Ms. Carla Nunez, reports that he plays alongside a classmate, Jaxon, during sensory bin time but does not yet initiate play verbally. Bath time, dinner, and a bedtime story routine with Miguel Reyes round out his evening before Fernanda Reyes Morales leaves for her shift.

6. OTHER AGENCIES AND COMMUNITY SUPPORTS

In addition to Foothills CDSA, the family receives ongoing support from WIC for nutrition supplementation and from Catawba County Department of Social Services for Medicaid case management. Fernanda Reyes Morales also connected with Smart Start of Catawba County for the parenting class referenced above. The family was referred to Catawba County Department of Social Services respite care services on August 14, 2026 and is currently on a waiting list. A family friend, Hector Lima, has offered to help with transportation to appointments when Rosa Morales is unavailable.

7. OUTCOMES, STRATEGIES, AND PROGRESS

Outcome 1: Dani will use five new single words consistently across home and Tumbleweed Treehouse Preschool settings to request preferred items within six months.
Strategies: Model target words during daily routines using Hanen "It Takes Two to Talk" strategies; pair spoken words with gesture; expand single-word attempts into two-word models (e.g., "more water"). Progress: at the time of this review, Dani has met criterion for three of the five targeted words with min to mod cues.

Outcome 2: Dani will combine two words to request or comment during play and mealtime routines, demonstrated in 3 of 5 opportunities across two consecutive sessions.
Strategies: Use PROMPT-informed tactile cueing for word-final consonants; caregiver coaching with Rosa Morales and Fernanda Reyes Morales on expansion and wait time. Progress: emerging, as noted in the "Sol up" and "Churro no" examples above; not yet consistent across settings.

Outcome 3: Dani will increase his consonant inventory to include word-initial stops and nasals in Spanish and English words with no more than mod cues.
Strategies: Target words selected jointly with the family, including sol, pan, and "ball," practiced through structured imitation and naturalistic play. text:
CONFIDENTIAL SPEECH-LANGUAGE EVALUATION REPORT

Piedmont Pediatric Therapy Associates
214 Churton Street, Hillsborough, NC 27278
Phone: (919) 555-0148 | Fax: (919) 555-0149

Client: Mateo Alexander Rivas-Fuentes (goes by "Teo")
Date of Birth: April 9, 2022
Chronological Age: 4;2
Evaluation Dates: June 11, 2026 and June 18, 2026
Report Date: June 22, 2026
Evaluating Clinician: Maria Hernandez-Lopez, M.S., CCC-SLP
Interpreter Present (Session 2): Carmen Diaz, certified medical interpreter
Referring Physician: Dr. Anjali Patel, Triangle Pediatrics
Service Coordinator: Keisha Brown, Orange County CDSA
Medicaid ID: 784512093B
Insurance Member ID: BCBSNC-55820147
NC ITP Child ID: NC-ITP-0048271
Authorization/Record #: Auth# 2026-11048

S: SUBJECTIVE

Reason for referral: Teo was referred by Dr. Patel after Teo's 4-year well-check flagged limited intelligibility and short utterance length. Mamá, Lucía Fuentes Morales, reports, "no le entiendo casi nada cuando está emocionado" (I can't understand almost anything he says when he's excited). Papá, Jonathan Rivas, agrees but notes Teo "se hace entender con las manos" (makes himself understood with his hands) and gestures a lot at home. A developmental screening done through Smart Start of Orange County in March 2026 also flagged concern, and the family was encouraged by a nutritionist at Orange County WIC during a routine visit to follow up on the referral promptly.

Birth and medical history: Teo was born at 38 weeks gestation via scheduled C-section at UNC Hillsborough Hospital. Birth weight 6 lbs 11 oz. Apgar scores 8 and 9. No NICU stay. Mom reports normal pregnancy, prenatal care through Orange County Health Department, no complications, "todo salió bien, gracias a Dios" (everything turned out fine, thank God). Hx of recurrent otitis media, 6 episodes between 8 months and 22 months, tx'd with abx each time. Bilateral PE tubes placed January 14, 2024 by Dr. Samuel Greene, ENT. No tubes currently in place; last ENT f/u March 3, 2026 noted resolved MEE bilaterally. No hx of seizures, head injury, or hospitalization beyond birth. Vision screening WNL per pediatrician record. Growth and feeding history unremarkable; mom denies any choking, gagging, or texture aversions, "come de todo, hasta lo picante" (he eats everything, even spicy food), though family jokes he is picky about mixing foods on his plate.

Family and language history: Household is bilingual Spanish-English. Primary caregivers are Lucía and Jonathan, married 6 years. Teo is the younger of two children; older sister Ariana Rivas, age 7, is a 2nd grader described as "muy habladora, al revés de su hermanito" (very talkative, opposite of her little brother). Ariana frequently interprets for Teo at home, finishing his sentences or answering for him when relatives ask him questions directly, which mom says she has started to discourage "para que él mismo hable" (so he talks for himself). Paternal grandmother, Rosa Morales ("Abuela Rosa"), lives with the family and provides after-school and evening childcare; she speaks mostly Spanish to Teo and reports he responds "pero casi no habla conmigo" (but he barely talks to me). A family friend, Yolanda Pérez, occasionally babysits on weekends when both parents' shifts overlap. At extended family gatherings, mom reports Teo tends to withdraw and play alone rather than join cousins, "se va para un lado solo con sus carritos" (he goes off to one side alone with his little cars).

Lucía works at Variedades La Esperanza, a general store, Tuesday through Saturday 8:30 AM to 4:00 PM; en español, ella "trabaja en la tienda Variedades La Esperanza" cerca de su casa. Jonathan works the overnight shift at Blue Ridge Poultry Processing, a poultry plant; "él trabaja en la planta de pollos Blue Ridge Poultry Processing" de 11:00 PM a 7:30 AM. Before the plant, Jonathan worked for several years at El Sabor Latino, a restaurant in Mebane; the family still says "trabajaba en el restaurante El Sabor Latino" when explaining why Teo's early routines were less consistent, since shift changes meant different relatives put him to bed on different nights. Abuela Rosa previously worked on a farm in her home country, Finca El Rocío ("trabajaba en la finca El Rocío"), before immigrating, and now helps mainly with childcare rather than outside work. Maternal aunt, Marisol Fuentes, works for a cleaning service, Brillante Cleaning Services ("trabaja en el servicio de limpieza Brillante Cleaning Services"), and her husband, Héctor Ramos, works for a construction company, Triangle Construction Company ("trabaja en la compañía de construcción Triangle Construction Company"). Both occasionally help with transportation to appointments when parents' schedules don't line up.

Teo attends El Jardín de los Soñadores, a bilingual early-learning program in Mebane, 7:45 AM to 5:15 PM, Monday through Friday. His lead teacher, Ms. Figueroa, reports he plays well in small groups but "se frustra y empuja cuando no lo entienden" (gets frustrated and pushes when they don't understand him). Classmates Dylan Ortiz and Camila Suárez are frequent play partners; Ms. Figueroa notes Camila often "habla por él" (talks for him) when adults ask questions, similar to the pattern mom described with Ariana at home. Assistant teacher Mr. Ruiz separately mentioned during pickup one afternoon that Teo "entiende todo lo que le decimos, solo que no contesta" (understands everything we tell him, he just doesn't answer). Family dog, Luna, is a favorite topic — Teo frequently points at her and says "Luna afuera" (Luna outside) rather than fuller phrases.

Mom reports Spanish is the dominant home language (~80% Spanish, 20% English), though Teo is increasingly exposed to English at El Jardín de los Soñadores and through Ariana, who code-switches constantly, often mid-sentence ("Teo, ven aquí, come here, vamos"). No concerns reported for Ariana's speech-language development; she met all milestones on time and was never referred for services. Family denies hx of ASD, hearing loss in extended family, or other developmental concerns, though mom notes a paternal uncle "no habló bien hasta los 5 años" (didn't speak well until age 5) and was eventually "dado de alta" (discharged) from services as a child, per family report, with no formal records available.

O: OBJECTIVE

Session 1 (June 11, 2026), conducted at Piedmont Pediatric Therapy Associates with Lucía present; no interpreter requested, mom comfortable in English for intake but code-switched throughout. Free play/rapport-building 9:00 AM–9:20 AM; structured standardized testing 9:20 AM–9:50 AM; brief snack break 9:50 AM–10:00 AM; parent interview and oral-mech/hearing screening 10:00 AM–10:15 AM.

Session 2 (June 18, 2026), testing completed with interpreter Carmen Diaz present for Spanish-language measures and parent report (SCQ-adapted interview). Jonathan attended this session on his day off. Spanish standardized testing 1:30 PM–2:00 PM; language sampling and stimulability probes 2:00 PM–2:30 PM; interpreter-supported parent interview 2:30 PM–2:45 PM.

Classroom observation: a brief informal observation was also completed by phone consultation with Ms. Figueroa on June 15, 2026 around 4:30 PM, in lieu of an in-person classroom visit, to corroborate parent and clinic findings.

Behavioral observations: Teo separated easily from mom, explored the therapy room, initiated play with blocks and a toy truck. Attention sustained ~12-15 minutes per activity with 1 break. Used gestures, pointing, and single words/short phrases to request and comment. Intelligibility estimated at 30-40% to unfamiliar listener (examiner) in connected speech, improving to 60% with context and gesture support. Oral mech exam WNL; no structural concerns, adequate DDK rates for age. Hearing screening passed bilaterally at 20 dB at 1000, 2000, and 4000 Hz today.

Standardized and informal measures administered:

Test/Measure | Language | Standard Score | Percentile | Age Equivalent
Preschool Language Scales-5 (PLS-5) Auditory Comprehension | English | 76 | 5th | 2;9
PLS-5 Expressive Communication | English | 68 | 2nd | 2;4
PLS-5 Total Language Score | English | 70 | 2nd | 2;6
Preschool Language Scales-5 Spanish (PLS-5 Spanish) Auditory Comprehension | Spanish | 82 | 12th | 3;1
PLS-5 Spanish Expressive Communication | Spanish | 79 | 8th | 2;10
PLS-5 Spanish Total Language Score | Spanish | 79 | 8th | 2;11
Goldman-Fristoe Test of Articulation-3 (GFTA-3) | English/Spanish combined | 65 | 1st | —
Bilingual English-Spanish Assessment (BESA) Phonology subtest | Both | 73-83 (CI) | 9th | —
Receptive-Expressive Emergent Language Test-4 (REEL-4) parent report | Both | 71 | 3rd | 2;7

Note: scores reflect 95% confidence intervals of 73-83 for BESA Phonology and 62-78 for PLS-5 English Total Language. Given bilingual exposure (~80/20 Spanish/English), composite scores in each single language likely underestimate true ability; conceptual scoring approach applied per BESA protocol where available, combining correct responses across both languages for a single, more representative score.

Articulation/phonology: Sound inventory includes stops, nasals, and most fricatives in both languages. Persisting error patterns: fronting of /k/ and /g/ (e.g., "tasa" for "casa"), stopping of /s/ and /z/ clusters, gliding of /ɾ/ and /l/ (e.g., "guapo" produced as "wapo"), final consonant deletion in English (e.g., "cat" → "ca"). PCC (percent consonants correct) estimated at 58% English, 64% Spanish, consistent with moderate-severe phonological disorder in both languages rather than a language-specific pattern, supporting a true SSD rather than a feature of normal bilingual development.

Expressive language sample (English, 50-utterance SALT analysis): MLU 2.1 morphemes, below expected range for age (3.5-4.5). Predominantly 2-word combinations ("more juice," "Luna outside," "no nap"). Frequent omission of grammatical morphemes; copula and auxiliary "be" absent in all obligatory contexts noted ([EW] coded 14 times for early word loss/omission on SALT transcript). Pronoun use limited to "me" and "yo"; no use of "he/she" or "él/ella" observed spontaneously. A shorter informal Spanish sample collected with interpreter support during Session 2 showed similar MLU in Spanish (2.3 morphemes), with frequent article omission ("quiero pelota" instead of "quiero la pelota") and inconsistent gender agreement on the few adjectives produced.

Receptive language: Followed 1-step directions consistently (9/10), 2-step directions inconsistently (4/10), struggled with directions containing spatial concepts (in/on/under) and quantity concepts (more/all/none), performing at 3 of 10 correct across both languages combined.

Social communication / pragmatics: Initiated joint attention and requests appropriately. Used gestures (pointing, reaching, pulling examiner's hand) to compensate for limited verbal output. Some frustration noted when unable to make needs known verbally — pushed toy away and vocalized loudly once during Session 1; redirected easily with moderate verbal cues. During a brief dyadic play probe with a peer-aged confederate toy, Teo took turns and shared materials without prompting, consistent with mom's report that peer play at El Jardín de los Soñadores is a relative strength. No repetitive behaviors, unusual sensory responses, or restricted interests noted. Eye contact and reciprocal play age-appropriate.

Stimulability/dynamic assessment: With maximal cueing, Teo produced /k/ correctly in isolation 7 of 10 trials and in CV syllables 3 of 10 trials. With minimal cues (visual + tactile), improved to 5 of 10 in CV context. Stimulable for /s/ in final position with moderate cues (6/10). Imitated 3-word models with mod cues on 4 of 6 trials, suggesting a reasonable zone of proximal development for expressive syntax goals.

Parent interview (via interpreter Carmen Diaz, Session 2): Jonathan reports concern began around 18 months when Teo "no decía casi nada, ni en español ni en inglés" (wasn't saying almost anything, in Spanish or English). First words reportedly emerged around 16-18 months, two-word combinations closer to 3;0 — both delayed relative to typical milestones. Family denies regression in skills. Lucía adds Teo understands routines and instructions in Spanish well at home, which the interpreter confirmed matches her own observation during the parent interview portion.

Collateral information: Per records release signed by Lucía Fuentes Morales on June 11, 2026, brief phone consult held with occupational therapist Jennifer Walsh, OTR/L, who has seen Teo monthly since February 2026 for fine motor delay; she reports improved pencil grasp and notes no oral-motor feeding concerns currently. Physical therapist Brian O'Connell, PT, DPT, discharged Teo from PT services on April 30, 2026 after meeting gross motor goals; his final note was reviewed with permission. Both providers coordinate through Orange County CDSA under the same IFSP.

A: ASSESSMENT

Teo presents with a moderate-severe speech sound disorder and moderate language delay evident in both English and Spanish, consistent with a true bilingual communication disorder rather than a difference attributable to second-language acquisition alone. Scores in each single language fall below expected limits (PLS-5 Total Language SS 70, 2nd percentile English; PLS-5 Spanish Total Language SS 79, 8th percentile Spanish), and deficits are present across both languages for phonology, expressive morphosyntax, and receptive concepts, which supports disorder over typical bilingual variability per current best-practice guidelines for bilingual assessment.

Differential considerations: Hx of recurrent OM with PE tubes is a plausible contributing factor to early phonological development, though current hearing is WNL, suggesting the disorder is unlikely to be purely conductive-hearing-loss-driven at this point. Social communication skills, joint attention, and play are age-appropriate, arguing against ASD as primary driver, though continued monitoring is reasonable given mild pragmatic frustration behaviors noted and family hx reported by mom (paternal uncle late talker). No oral-motor or structural findings suggest CAS as primary diagnosis, though inconsistent error patterns across repeated trials on stimulability testing warrant continued rule-out monitoring; recommend differentiating SSD-with-phonological-pattern vs. CAS features at reassessment if progress is atypically slow, particularly given the variability noted between isolation and CV-context trials for /k/.

ICD-10: F80.1 (Expressive Language Disorder), F80.0 (Phonological Disorder), rule out F80.2 (Mixed Receptive-Expressive Language Disorder) pending further receptive-language follow-up given inconsistent 2-step direction-following.

CPT codes for today's services: 92523 (speech sound production with evaluation of language), 96127 (brief emotional/behavioral screen, pragmatics checklist).

Teo meets eligibility criteria for ongoing speech-language intervention under NC Infant-Toddler Program / Part C given scores more than 1.5 SD below the mean in 2+ domains in both languages tested. Severity is judged moderate-severe for phonology and moderate for expressive/receptive language, with prognosis judged good given strong stimulability, intact social communication, and a supportive, motivated family.

P: PLAN

1. Recommend speech-language therapy 2x/week, 30 minutes individual sessions, targeting:
   - Phonological process remediation (fronting, stopping, gliding, final consonant deletion) using a Cycles approach across both languages with bilingual minimal pairs where possible.
   - Expressive syntax growth targeting 3-4 word utterances, copula/auxiliary "be," and basic pronouns, incorporating PROMPT tactile cueing given stimulability data.
   - Receptive concept vocabulary (spatial/quantity terms) in both languages.
   - Continued support for augmentative gesture use and introduction of a modified PECS-based visual support system to reduce frustration during the transition period while verbal skills build.

2. Recommend caregiver coaching using a Hanen-based ("It Takes Two to Talk") framework, delivered bilingually, with specific strategies for Abuela Rosa and both parents given differing schedules; home program materials to be provided in Spanish so Abuela Rosa and Lucía can practice during the day while Jonathan sleeps before his overnight shift.

3. Continue coordination with Jennifer Walsh, OTR/L, and service coordinator Keisha Brown at Orange County CDSA for IFSP update; propose adding speech-language Outcome #3 ("Teo will use 3-4 word phrases to request and comment across settings") at next 6-month review, tentatively scheduled December 10, 2026.

4. Request updated audiological monitoring given hx of recurrent OM; f/u with Dr. Samuel Greene or current ENT if any new episodes occur.

5. Share written summary (bilingual) with El Jardín de los Soñadores and Ms. Figueroa to support classroom carryover strategies, with signed release on file dated June 11, 2026. Encourage Mr. Ruiz to continue offering Teo choices verbally rather than accepting pointing alone, to build expressive output opportunities throughout the school day.

6. Discussed with family the option of a short home-practice routine (5-10 minutes, 4-5x/week) built around daily moments already happening — walking Luna, riding in the car to El Jardín de los Soñadores — rather than a separate structured activity, given parents' limited overlapping free time.

7. Re-evaluate formally in 6 months (~December 2026) or sooner if progress is slower than expected, to reassess CAS rule-out status and update standardized scores.

8. Family was given clinic's after-hours contact (919) 555-0148 and encouraged to call with questions; email summary sent to lucia.fuentesmorales@example.com per parent request. Next scheduled therapy session: June 25, 2026, 9:30 AM.

Discussed findings and recommendations with Lucía Fuentes Morales and Jonathan Rivas in person (Session 2) with interpreter support; both expressed understanding and agreement with plan. Mom stated, "quiero que hable los dos idiomas, español e inglés, no quiero que pierda ninguno" (I want him to speak both languages, Spanish and English, I don't want him to lose either one) — goal incorporated into bilingual treatment approach above. Dad added that he is willing to rearrange his schedule at Blue Ridge Poultry Processing on session days if transportation becomes an issue, and offered Héctor Ramos as a backup driver since his schedule at Triangle Construction Company is more flexible.

Report prepared by: Maria Hernandez-Lopez, M.S., CCC-SLP
Piedmont Pediatric Therapy Associates
Date: June 22, 2026
