INFORME DE EVALUACIÓN DEL HABLA Y DEL LENGUAJE

Nombre del niño: Mateo Alejandro Cruz Ramírez (le dicen "Teo")
Fecha de nacimiento: 14 de marzo de 2022
Edad cronológica en el momento de la evaluación: 4;7
Fecha de evaluación: 9 de octubre de 2026
Número de expediente: CPT-4471829
Número de Medicaid: MC8827341C
Distrito escolar: Distrito Escolar del Condado de Pinnacle
Escuela: Escuela Primaria Pinnacle Ridge
Salón: Salón 14, a cargo de la maestra Carmen Boyd; auxiliar de salón, Miss Ana
Patóloga del habla y del lenguaje: Patricia Elena Flores Vega, M.S., CCC-SLP, bilingüe español-inglés
Compañía: Carolina Bilingual Speech & Language Therapy, PLLC
Pediatra remitente: Dr. James Patterson
Coordinadora de servicios: Karen Phillips, CDSA del Condado de Pinnacle

RAZÓN DE LA REMISIÓN

Teo fue remitido para esta evaluación por su pediatra, el Dr. James Patterson, y por la maestra Carmen Boyd, quien notó que Mateo habla mucho menos que sus compañeros de salón y que con frecuencia señala en vez de usar palabras. La evaluación se llevó a cabo en las oficinas de Carolina Bilingual Speech & Language Therapy, PLLC, ubicadas en 118 Harmon Street, Burlington, NC 27217. La sesión comenzó a las 9:30 a.m. y duró dos horas y media. Durante la cita estuvieron presentes Teo y su mamá, Lucía Ramírez Torres.

ANTECEDENTES PRENATALES, DEL NACIMIENTO Y MÉDICOS

Según el reporte de Lucía Ramírez Torres, el embarazo de Teo fue de término, sin complicaciones mayores, aunque ella reporta haber tenido presión alta leve durante el tercer trimestre, controlada sin medicamento. Mateo nació a las 39 semanas de gestación por parto vaginal en el Hospital Regional Pinnacle Valley, con un peso de 3,180 gramos y Apgar de 9 al minuto y 9 a los cinco minutos. No requirió tiempo en cuidados intensivos neonatales. Su desarrollo motor fue típico: caminó sin apoyo a los 13 meses. Los hitos del lenguaje se retrasaron: según la mamá, Teo dijo sus primeras palabras alrededor de los 22 meses, y hasta la fecha combina solo dos o tres palabras en frases cortas.

El historial médico incluye dos episodios de otitis media aguda, uno a los 18 meses y otro a los 26 meses, tratados con antibiótico sin necesidad de tubos de ventilación. Una prueba de audición realizada el 3 de febrero de 2026 en el consultorio del Dr. James Patterson resultó dentro de límites normales en ambos oídos. No hay diagnóstico de autismo ni de pérdida auditiva permanente. Mateo recibe actualmente servicios de intervención temprana coordinados por CDSA del Condado de Pinnacle bajo la Resultado 2 de su Plan Individualizado de Servicios para la Familia, enfocado en comunicación funcional, y la Resultado 3, enfocada en juego con sus compañeros.

HISTORIA FAMILIAR Y DEL LENGUAJE

Teo vive con su mamá, Lucía Ramírez Torres, su papá, Jorge Cruz Delgado, y su hermana mayor, Camila, de siete años, en una casa ubicada en 482 Willowbrook Lane, Burlington, NC 27215, dentro del condado de Pinnacle. La familia también cuenta con la ayuda de la abuela materna, Rosa Torres, quien vive a pocas cuadras y cuida a los niños algunas tardes, y de la niñera de confianza, doña Lupe, quien recoge a Teo de la escuela los días que los papás trabajan hasta tarde. En casa también vive el perro de la familia, Rocky, al que Teo señala y llama "guau guau" en vez de decir su nombre.

Lucía Ramírez Torres nació en una vereda pequeña llamada El Progreso, cerca del municipio de San Marcos, en Honduras, donde su familia trabajaba en la finca familiar conocida como la finca La Esperanza, cultivando café y maíz. Emigró a los Estados Unidos hace nueve años y se estableció primero en Florida antes de mudarse a Carolina del Norte. Jorge Cruz Delgado es originario de un pueblo cercano a San Pedro Sula y llegó al país hace once años. En casa se habla principalmente español; Lucía reporta que ella le habla a Teo siempre en español, mientras que Jorge alterna entre español e inglés, sobre todo cuando repite instrucciones que escucha en su trabajo. Camila es completamente bilingüe y suele traducir para Teo cuando él se frustra porque no lo entienden en inglés.

Actualmente Lucía Ramírez Torres trabaja de mesera en el restaurante El Buen Sabor, con turnos que a veces se extienden hasta las nueve de la noche. Antes de este trabajo, ella trabajó varios años en la tienda Dollar Max, cerca de su casa, doblando turnos de fin de semana. Jorge Cruz Delgado trabaja actualmente en Pine Valley Construction Company, bajo la supervisión de un capataz al que todos en la cuadrilla llaman Mr. Tom; antes de eso trabajó varios años en Carolina Poultry Processing Plant, procesando pollo en turnos de noche, lo cual limitaba el tiempo que pasaba con los niños. La tía de Teo, Marta Torres, trabaja en el servicio de limpieza Luz y Brillo, limpiando oficinas por las noches, y a veces se queda con los niños los fines de semana.

En la escuela, Teo asiste al programa de preescolar del distrito en Escuela Primaria Pinnacle Ridge, en el salón de la maestra Carmen Boyd. Sus compañeros de clase incluyen a Ethan, con quien juega en el área de bloques, y a Sofía, quien según la maestra suele hablar por él cuando él no logra pedir lo que quiere. La familia reporta que Teo disfruta mucho ir a la escuela y que llora cuando tiene que faltar.

OBSERVACIONES CONDUCTUALES

Durante la evaluación, Teo se mostró activo, curioso y con buen contacto visual. Se separó de su mamá sin dificultad para explorar los juguetes en la sala de evaluación. Su juego fue principalmente funcional y simbólico simple; por ejemplo, alimentó a un muñeco y dijo "bebé come". Mostró atención sostenida de aproximadamente ocho a diez minutos por actividad antes de necesitar un cambio de tarea. No se observaron conductas repetitivas ni dificultades sensoriales significativas. Respondió bien a instrucciones simples acompañadas de gestos, pero mostró mayor dificultad con instrucciones de dos pasos sin apoyo visual.

RESULTADOS DE LAS PRUEBAS ESTANDARIZADAS

Se administraron las siguientes pruebas en español, con apoyo de materiales bilingües cuando fue apropiado:

Preschool Language Scale, Fifth Edition, Spanish (PLS-5 Spanish)
- Comprensión Auditiva: puntaje estándar 78, percentil 7, intervalo de confianza del 95% 71–85, edad equivalente 3;2–3;6
- Comunicación Expresiva: puntaje estándar 73, percentil 4, intervalo de confianza del 95% 66–80, edad equivalente 2;9–3;1
- Puntaje Total del Lenguaje: puntaje estándar 74, percentil 4, intervalo de confianza del 95% 68–80

Bilingual English Spanish Assessment (BESA)
- Subprueba de Morfosintaxis (español): percentil 9, rango descriptivo "por debajo del promedio"
- Subprueba de Vocabulario (español): percentil 15, rango descriptivo "levemente por debajo del promedio"
- Puntaje compuesto bilingüe: percentil 11

Goldman-Fristoe Test of Articulation, Third Edition (GFTA-3)
- Puntaje estándar: 81, percentil 10, intervalo de confianza del 95% 75–87
- Edad equivalente: 3;6–3;10

Análisis fonológico: Teo sustituye los sonidos /k/ y /g/ por [t] y [d] respectivamente (por ejemplo, dice "tasa" por "casa" y "dato" por "gato"), y omite el sonido /s/ final en la mayoría de las palabras. También simplifica los grupos consonánticos, produciendo "poto" por "plato". Su inteligibilidad fue de aproximadamente 60% para oyentes familiares y menor para oyentes que no lo conocen bien.

Muestra de lenguaje espontáneo: se obtuvo una muestra de 50 enunciados durante el juego libre. La longitud media de enunciado fue de 2.3 morfemas, considerablemente por debajo de lo esperado para su edad. Teo combinó dos palabras en el 8 de 10 de los enunciados elegibles, y usó estructuras de tres palabras en solo 3 de 20 oportunidades. Produjo de manera espontánea frases como "mamá dame" y "Teo quiere agua", esta última con apoyo de un modelo mod cues de la evaluadora.

Comprensión: en tareas de seguimiento de instrucciones de dos pasos sin gesto, Teo respondió correctamente en 4 de 10 intentos. Con apoyo visual (señalando objetos), su desempeño mejoró a 8 de 10. En identificación de vocabulario receptivo, nombró o señaló correctamente 18 de 20 ítems presentados.

IMPRESIONES CLÍNICAS

Los resultados de esta evaluación indican que Mateo Alejandro Cruz Ramírez presenta un trastorno del lenguaje expresivo y receptivo de grado moderado, junto con un trastorno de los sonidos del habla, también de grado moderado, en el contexto de un desarrollo bilingüe típico. Es importante destacar que las dificultades de Teo se observan tanto en español, su idioma dominante en casa, como en las muestras limitadas de inglés obtenidas durante la sesión, lo cual sugiere un patrón consistente con un trastorno primario del lenguaje y no simplemente con una diferencia esperada por la adquisición de dos idiomas. Diagnóstico correspondiente: F80.2 (trastorno mixto del lenguaje receptivo-expresivo) e F80.0 (trastorno fonológico).

Las fortalezas de Teo incluyen buen contacto visual, interés social en sus compañeros como Ethan, y una base sólida de juego simbólico que puede aprovecharse como vehículo para intervenir en el lenguaje. Su familia está muy involucrada: tanto Lucía Ramírez Torres como Jorge Cruz Delgado reportan practicar actividades de lenguaje en casa pese a sus horarios de trabajo exigentes, y figuras de apoyo como doña Lupe y la abuela Rosa Torres también interactúan con él frecuentemente.

RECOMENDACIONES

1. Se recomienda terapia de habla y lenguaje individual, dos veces por semana, sesiones de 30 minutos, con enfoque bilingüe español-inglés, en coordinación con CDSA del Condado de Pinnacle y la Resultado 2 del IFSP actual.

2. Se recomienda el uso del enfoque Hanen para entrenar a Lucía Ramírez Torres y Jorge Cruz Delgado en estrategias de estimulación del lenguaje en el hogar, adaptadas a sus horarios de trabajo en el restaurante El Buen Sabor y en Pine Valley Construction Company.

3. Para el componente fonológico, se recomienda el enfoque de Cycles dirigido a los patrones de sustitución de /k/ y /g/ y a la simplificación de grupos consonánticos, iniciando con nivel de claves de tipo cues moderadas (mod cues) y reduciendo el apoyo según el progreso.

4. Se recomienda consulta con la maestra Carmen Boyd y Miss Ana para incorporar estrategias de apoyo visual en el salón de Escuela Primaria Pinnacle Ridge, y considerar el uso de tableros de comunicación tipo PECS durante actividades grupales mientras mejora el lenguaje expresivo de Teo.

5. Se recomienda nueva evaluación auditiva de seguimiento con el Dr. James Patterson si se observan nuevos episodios de otitis media, dado el historial de infecciones a los 18 y 26 meses.

6. Se recomienda reevaluación formal en seis meses, o antes si Teo hace la transición a servicios escolares de preescolar especial, para actualizar los puntajes y ajustar los objetivos del plan de tratamiento.

Esta evaluación fue realizada y este informe fue preparado por Patricia Elena Flores Vega, M.S., CCC-SLP, patóloga del habla y del lenguaje bilingüe, de Carolina Bilingual Speech & Language Therapy, PLLC. Para preguntas sobre este informe, favor comunicarse al (336) 555-0147 o al correo pflores@carolinabilingualslt.com.

text:
+ Name: Mateo del Río
+ CA: 2;4 (28 months)
+ Context: Annual IFSP Review, home visit and clinic observation, conducted by Daniela Ortiz-Flores, M.S., CCC-SLP, bilingual speech-language pathologist with Sandhills Pediatric Therapy Services, PLLC, in collaboration with Brenda Hodges, Service Coordinator, Sandhills CDSA. Spanish/English bilingual household.

Resumen / Summary: This report documents the annual IFSP review for Mateo del Río, a Spanish/English bilingual toddler born at 32 weeks gestational age with a birth weight of 1,680 grams and Apgar scores of 5 and 7. Mateo was followed in the Sandhills Regional Health – Sandhills Children's Hospital, Hope Mills Campus NICU for six weeks and has since been seen for routine follow-up at Sandhills Pediatrics, Fayetteville Office. He presents with delayed expressive language, limited intelligible vocabulary, and an emerging oral-motor speech sound disorder consistent with the phonological process profile targeted in the Cycles approach. This review was conducted in the family home at 214 Persimmon Lane, Hope Mills, Cumberland County, on 3 de marzo de 2025, at 9:15 a.m., with Carla Fuentes (madre) present and Andrés del Río (padre) joining by phone at 9:40 a.m..

Historia y Contexto Familiar / Family Background

Mateo lives with his parents, Carla Fuentes and Andrés del Río, and his two siblings, Diego del Río (age 7) and Sol del Río (age 5), in a rented home near downtown Hope Mills. His maternal grandmother, Doña Rosa Fuentes, lives two doors down and provides childcare several afternoons a week while Carla works a shift at the Smithfield Foods processing plant in Dunn. Andrés works full-time at the Goodyear tire plant in Fayetteville and is often unavailable for daytime appointments, which is why today's review included him by phone. The family identifies Spanish as the primary home language; Carla reports, "en casa hablamos puro español, pero los niños ya mezclan mucho con el inglés de la escuela" (at home we speak pure Spanish, but the kids already mix a lot with the English from school). Diego and Sol both attend Hope Mills Elementary, and Sol is in kindergarten.

Reason for Referral and Early History

Mateo was referred to Sandhills CDSA shortly after NICU discharge due to prematurity and feeding difficulties. He was born on 14 de agosto de 2023 (08/14/2023) and discharged from the NICU on 09/28/2023. Following discharge, he was followed by audiology at Carolina Ear, Nose & Throat and Audiology Associates, Hope Mills Office, where a diagnostic ABR on 12/02/2023 ruled out sensorineural hearing loss bilaterally. An interpreter, Marisol Peña, assisted the family during that audiology visit and has continued to support communication at several subsequent appointments. The initial IFSP was developed on el martes 4 de junio de 2024, with the most recent periodic review completed on 11/14/2024. Today's annual review is being completed on 3 de marzo de 2025, with the next review due by 09/04/2025.

Preocupaciones y Prioridades de la Familia / Family Concerns and Priorities

Carla reports, "mi mayor preocupación es que Mateo no habla casi nada, solo dice "mamá" y "papá" y a veces "agua"" (my biggest worry is that Mateo barely talks at all; he only says "mama" and "papa" and sometimes "water"). She also shared, "se frustra mucho cuando no lo entendemos, grita y se tira al piso" (he gets very frustrated when we don't understand him; he screams and throws himself on the floor). Andrés added by phone, "yo quiero que aprenda a jugar mejor con sus hermanos, que Diego y Sol no lo dejen fuera" (I want him to learn to play better with his siblings, so Diego and Sol don't leave him out). The family's top priorities for this IFSP year are: (1) functional expressive vocabulary in both languages, (2) reduced frustration-related behavior, and (3) improved play interaction with Diego and Sol.

Rutinas Diarias / Daily Routines

Carla described a typical day: Mateo wakes around 7:30 a.m., eats breakfast with the family, and is cared for by Doña Rosa while Carla works her shift. In the afternoon, Doña Rosa takes him and his dog, Capitán, for a walk around the block, which Carla says is one of his favorite routines. Dinner is a family meal at 6:00 p.m., followed by bath time and a bedtime routine around 8:00 p.m. that includes reading a picture book in Spanish. Carla noted that Mateo points and grunts to request snacks and toys rather than using words, and that transitions, such as leaving the park, are a common trigger for tantrums.

Otras Agencias Involucradas / Other Agencies

In addition to Sandhills CDSA, the family receives nutrition support through Cumberland County WIC and has enrolled Mateo in a part-time program through Fayetteville Early Head Start beginning this spring. Carla also mentioned contact with Cumberland Smart Start for a parenting class referral. Brenda Hodges coordinates across these agencies and can be reached at (910) 555-0147. Daniela Ortiz-Flores can be reached at dortizflores@sandhillspeds.org or through the agency portal at www.sandhillscdsa.org.

Evaluation Summary

On 02/18/2025, Mateo was assessed using the Preschool Language Scales, Fifth Edition (PLS-5) Spanish/English bilingual administration. Auditory Comprehension standard score was 68 (2nd percentile); Expressive Communication standard score was 62 (1st percentile); age equivalents fell in the range of 11-14 months. Articulation screening showed consistent final consonant deletion and stopping of fricatives, with intelligibility estimated at 30% to unfamiliar listeners and 60% to familiar listeners. During structured play, Mateo attempted the target word "sol" (sun) with 90% accuracy using mod cues, producing [so] with the targeted final consonant deletion pattern addressed under the Cycles approach this quarter. Later in the session, when his older sister entered the room, Mateo looked up and said Sol "ta" (Sol's here), pointing toward her — his first spontaneous two-word combination directed at a family member noted this quarter.

Current IFSP Outcomes and Strategies

Outcome 1: Mateo will use 20 functional single words across both languages during daily routines, as reported by caregivers, by the next review. Strategy: phonological therapy using the Cycles approach, targeting final consonant deletion and stopping patterns across a rotating word list, with home practice coached in both English and Spanish. Progress: at initial baseline 3 of 20 target words were produced; at this review, 9 of 20 (45%) target words are produced with mod cues to min cues.

Outcome 2: Carla and Andrés will use responsive communication strategies during daily play to increase Mateo's initiations. Strategy: coaching sessions based on the Hanen program It Takes Two to Talk, focused on following Mateo's lead, expanding his utterances ("sol" → "quiero sol" / "I want sun"), and building in wait time during routines such as snack and bath. Carla reported, "ya sé esperar más antes de hablar por él" (I already know to wait more before speaking for him), reflecting increased carryover of strategies between sessions.

Outcome 3: Mateo will reduce frustration-related behavior during communication breakdowns from 8 episodes per day to 3 or fewer, as tracked by caregiver log. Strategy: introduction of a core board and PECS exchange cards as a backup modality for high-demand moments (snack, more, help, outside), paired with PROMPT tactile-kinesthetic cueing to support jaw and lip placement for imitated words during structured sessions. Progress: caregiver log shows a decrease from 8 to 4 daily episodes over the past 6 weeks, with Mateo independently retrieving the "more" card 7 of 10 opportunities.

Outcome 4: Mateo will engage in reciprocal play routines with Diego and Sol for at least 5 minutes without adult prompting, 3 times per week. Strategy: structured sibling play sessions incorporating PECS cards and simple turn-taking scripts, with elements of the Kaufman (Kaufman Speech to Language Protocol) hierarchy used to shape approximations of play-related words such as "mi turno" (my turn) and his sister's name. Andrés noted, "Sol ya sabe esperar y le enseña las tarjetas" (Sol already knows to wait and shows him the cards), indicating generalization of strategies to sibling interaction outside of therapy.

Recomendaciones / Recommendations

Given continued delays across both languages, continued direct speech-language therapy is recommended at a frequency of 2 sessions per week, 30 minutes each, split between home and the clinic setting at Sandhills Pediatrics, Fayetteville Office. The team recommends continued bilingual service delivery, as the family's primary language is Spanish and both parents have requested that strategies be modeled in Spanish first, then transitioned into English as appropriate for the daycare and school settings Diego and Sol attend. A referral to occupational therapy for sensory regulation during transitions was discussed and will be pursued through Sandhills CDSA if frustration behaviors do not continue to decrease.

Service Coordinator: Brenda Hodges, Sandhills CDSA, (910) 555-0147
Speech-Language Pathologist: Daniela Ortiz-Flores, M.S., CCC-SLP, Sandhills Pediatric Therapy Services, PLLC, (910) 555-0289
Current IFSP Period: 11/14/2024 through 09/04/2025
Next Review Due: 09/04/2025

Sign-off

This review was completed in the family home at 214 Persimmon Lane, Hope Mills, Cumberland County, 28348, on 3 de marzo de 2025. Both parents verbally consented to the continuation of services and strategies outlined above. Carla Fuentes signed the IFSP review form in the presence of Daniela Ortiz-Flores and Brenda Hodges; Andrés del Río provided verbal consent by phone, to be followed by a mailed signature page.

text:
+ Name: Mateo Alejandro de la Cruz
+ CA: 4;2
+ Context: Comprehensive bilingual speech-language evaluation completed at Novant Health Pediatric Rehabilitation at Forsyth Medical Center, Winston-Salem, to update eligibility and treatment planning. Evaluation conducted in English and Spanish across two sessions in the clinic and one home observation. Interpreter support provided by Marisol Peña, contracted bilingual interpreter.

SUMMARY

Mateo is a 4;2-year-old bilingual Spanish/English-speaking boy referred by his pediatrician, Dr. Howard Ellison, and his service coordinator, Teresa Guzmán, of the Centro de Desarrollo Infantil del Área de Piedmont (CDSA Piedmont), for re-evaluation of expressive and receptive language skills prior to his third-year transition IFSP review. Mateo currently receives speech-language therapy twice weekly through CDSA Piedmont under IFSP outcome #3 and attends Little Sprouts Bilingual Daycare in Kernersville, where he is enrolled in Ms. Lopez's room. His family also receives nutritional support through WIC and case management through the Forsyth County Department of Social Services (DSS). This evaluation was requested to document present levels of functioning and to inform recommendations as Mateo approaches his third birthday and potential transition to preschool special education services.

BACKGROUND

Mateo was born on June 14, 2022, at Atrium Health Wake Forest Baptist Medical Center in Winston-Salem, to Lucía de la Cruz and Esteban Rivas-Molina. He was born at 34 weeks gestational age following a pregnancy complicated by preeclampsia, with a birth weight of 4 lbs 6 oz and Apgar scores of 6 and 8 at one and five minutes. Mateo spent 19 days in the Brenner Children's Hospital Neonatal Intensive Care Unit for respiratory distress and feeding support, including a short course of CPAP and a nasogastric tube. He was followed by the NICU follow-up clinic through 18 months of age, with his final visit noted in records dated December 9, 2023.

Medical history is significant for three episodes of acute otitis media between 8 and 20 months of age, managed with antibiotics, and a referral to Novant Health ENT & Allergy – Hanes Mall Campus for evaluation. Tympanostomy tubes were placed on April 2, 2024, by Dr. Priya Subramaniam, with resolution of recurrent infections. A follow-up audiological evaluation at Novant Health Audiology at Hanes Mall on July 11, 2024 documented bilateral hearing within normal limits (pure tone thresholds 10-15 dB HL) and normal tympanometry bilaterally. No further ENT concerns are reported at this time.

Mateo was initially referred to CDSA Piedmont (formally, Centro de Desarrollo Infantil del Área de Piedmont) at 10 months of age due to feeding difficulties and delayed babbling, identified during a NICU follow-up visit. His case was opened with service coordinator Teresa Guzmán, who has coordinated his IFSP since initial eligibility on April 20, 2023. His most recent annual IFSP review occurred on March 3, 2026, at which time goals in expressive language (IFSP outcome #3) and feeding/oral-motor skills (IFSP outcome #5) were updated.

FAMILY AND LANGUAGE HISTORY

Mateo lives with his mother, Lucía de la Cruz, his father, Esteban Rivas-Molina, and his older sister, Valentina Rivas, age 7, who attends Clemmons Elementary School. His maternal grandmother, Rosa del Río, lives with the family part-time and provides childcare several days a week, primarily speaking Spanish with Mateo. Family history is also notable for a paternal uncle, Joaquín Rivas-Molina, who was diagnosed with a language disorder in childhood.

The home language environment is primarily Spanish, with Lucía reporting approximately 70% Spanish and 30% English input at home. Esteban works at Herbalife Manufacturing in Winston-Salem and reports speaking mostly English at work but Spanish at home. Lucía previously received support from Smart Start of Forsyth County for early literacy materials and currently participates in a parent support group facilitated through Early Head Start at the Union Cross site. The family's WIC caseworker, Brenda Collazo, has supported nutritional counseling related to Mateo's feeding history.

At Little Sprouts Bilingual Daycare, Mateo is described by his teacher, Ms. Lopez, as social and eager to interact with peers but difficult to understand, particularly in multi-word utterances. Ms. Lopez reports that Mateo frequently plays with a classmate, Diego Fuentes, and often gestures or points when peers do not understand him. The family's previous pediatric speech therapist, Hannah Weigel, of Carolina Pediatric Therapy Associates, provided six months of private speech therapy prior to the current CDSA-funded services, with records transferred on January 15, 2025.

BEHAVIORAL OBSERVATIONS

Mateo presented as a friendly, curious child who separated easily from his mother and engaged readily with the examiner and interpreter. He transitioned well between activities with occasional need for a visual schedule. Attention to structured tasks was adequate for approximately 15-20 minutes before requiring a movement break. Mateo used a mix of gestures, single words, and short two-word combinations to communicate, with intelligibility estimated at approximately 40% to unfamiliar listeners and 65% to familiar listeners in context. He demonstrated frustration when not understood, occasionally pulling at the examiner's sleeve or pointing to desired items.

During free play, Mateo referenced his family dog, saying "Milo afuera" (translated: "Milo outside"), demonstrating emerging two-word combinations in Spanish. He also attempted to name a toy truck, producing "tuck" for truck, substituting a stop for the final consonant cluster.

ASSESSMENT RESULTS

Standardized and criterion-referenced measures were administered in both English and Spanish, with results interpreted in the context of Mateo's bilingual language environment.

The Preschool Language Scales, Fifth Edition (PLS-5) was administered in English and Spanish forms with the following results:

Domain | English Standard Score | Spanish Standard Score | Percentile (combined)
Auditory Comprehension | 78 | 85 | 16th percentile
Expressive Communication | 70 | 74 | 5th percentile
Total Language Score | 73 | 79 | 8th percentile

Confidence intervals for the Total Language Score ranged from 68-78 (English) and 74-84 (Spanish), both falling within the moderately delayed range relative to age expectations. Age equivalents for expressive language fell between 2;0 and 2;6, reflecting a gap of approximately 18-24 months relative to chronological age.

The Goldman-Fristoe Test of Articulation, Third Edition (GFTA-3) was administered in English, yielding a standard score of 65 (1st percentile), with a Sounds-in-Words raw score reflecting multiple phonological process errors including final consonant deletion, cluster reduction, and fronting. Spanish phonological skills were assessed informally using a Spanish articulation screening, revealing similar patterns of final consonant deletion and cluster reduction consistent with a phonological disorder rather than a language-specific difference.

Specific error patterns observed included substitution of /t/ for /k/ in word-initial position (e.g., "tat" for "cat"), deletion of final consonants (e.g., "ca" for "cat"), and cluster reduction (e.g., "poon" for "spoon"). Mateo produced the target word "ball" as "baw," demonstrating liquid gliding of /l/ to [w]. In Spanish, he produced "pelo" for "perro," showing substitution of the trilled /r/ with the lateral /l/, a pattern that may reflect both phonological process and typical developmental variation in Spanish-speaking children his age.

An oral-motor examination revealed adequate structure and function for speech, with mildly reduced diadochokinetic rates. No concerns were noted regarding feeding at this time, consistent with resolution of earlier feeding difficulties addressed under IFSP outcome #5.

A language sample was collected during structured and unstructured play, yielding a mean length of utterance (MLU) of 1.8 morphemes in English and 2.1 morphemes in Spanish. SALT analysis coding indicated frequent use of [EW] (errored word) codes for substituted or omitted grammatical morphemes, and [EO] codes for omitted obligatory forms such as articles and plural markers.

Parent report via the MacArthur-Bates Communicative Development Inventories (CDI), Spanish-English bilingual version, indicated an expressive vocabulary of approximately 85 words combined across both languages, below the 10th percentile for bilingual peers of similar age and language exposure.

IMPRESSIONS

Mateo presents with a mixed receptive-expressive language disorder and a moderate phonological disorder affecting intelligibility in both English and Spanish. His language profile is consistent with a true language impairment rather than a language difference attributable to bilingual exposure, as deficits are observed across both languages relative to monolingual and bilingual normative data. His phonological error patterns (final consonant deletion, cluster reduction, stopping, gliding) are present in both languages and are not accounted for by typical cross-linguistic transfer patterns alone.

Mateo continues to meet eligibility criteria for early intervention services under current North Carolina criteria, with standard scores more than 1.5 standard deviations below the mean in both receptive and expressive domains. Given his age (4;2), his family should be informed of the upcoming transition process to preschool special education services through the local school district, as he will likely require continued speech-language services beyond his third birthday.

RECOMMENDATIONS

1. Continue individual speech-language therapy twice weekly, transitioning service delivery model as appropriate given Mateo's approaching transition out of Part C services.

2. Target phonological processes using a cycles-based approach (Cycles) addressing final consonant deletion and cluster reduction across both English and Spanish contexts, given cross-linguistic error patterns.

3. Incorporate PROMPT tactile-kinesthetic cueing strategies to support improved oral-motor placement for target sounds, particularly /k/, /l/, and consonant clusters.

4. Continue bilingual language stimulation in the home using Hanen "It Takes Two to Talk" strategies, with coaching provided to Lucía de la Cruz and Esteban Rivas-Molina during home visits.

5. Collaborate with Little Sprouts Bilingual Daycare staff, including Ms. Lopez, to implement classroom-based language supports, including visual schedules and peer-modeling strategies with classmates such as Diego Fuentes.

6. Refer family to CDSA Piedmont service coordinator Teresa Guzmán for discussion of transition planning, including notification to the local school district at least 90 days prior to Mateo's third birthday.

7. Recommend repeat audiological monitoring given history of recurrent otitis media, with follow-up at Novant Health Audiology at Hanes Mall in 6 months or sooner if concerns arise.

8. Provide family with bilingual home practice materials, coordinated with Early Head Start parent support group and WIC caseworker Brenda Collazo as appropriate for continuity of care.

9. Re-evaluate in 6 months or at the time of transition planning meeting, whichever occurs first, to update present levels and inform eligibility determination for the local school district.

This evaluation was completed with interpreter support from Marisol Peña. Results were reviewed with the family in Spanish and English, and a written summary will be provided in both languages. Please direct questions to this clinician at j.kowalczyk@novanthealthslp.org or (336) 555-0147.

Service Coordinator: Teresa Hinojosa, Guilford County CDSA office

REASON FOR REFERRAL

Mateo was referred for a comprehensive bilingual speech-language evaluation by his pediatrician, Dr. Anand, and his service coordinator at the Guilford County CDSA office, Teresa Hinojosa, because of limited and unclear speech, reduced vocabulary in both of his languages, and difficulty following multi-step directions at home and in his Early Head Start classroom. His mother, Lucía Flores-Martínez, reported that Mateo's speech is "harder to understand than his sister's was at his age," and that unfamiliar listeners, including her own mother, often ask her to repeat what he says. This evaluation was requested to determine Mateo's current speech and language skills in Spanish and English, to describe his eligibility for services under Part C of IDEA, and to guide goals for his Individualized Family Service Plan (IFSP).

This is Mateo's initial comprehensive evaluation. He was seen for two sessions, one hour each, at the Piedmont Bilingual Speech & Language Associates office on October 2, 2026 and October 6, 2026. Sandra Núñez interpreted during both sessions and assisted with Spanish-language test administration and family interview. Lucía Flores-Martínez and Mateo's father, Andrés de la Cruz, were both present for the first session; only Lucía attended the second session because Andrés was at work.

BACKGROUND INFORMATION

Birth and Medical History

Mateo was born at 37 weeks gestation by scheduled cesarean section at Cone Health Women's Hospital in Greensboro. Birth weight was 5 lbs 14 oz, and Apgar scores were 8 and 9 at one and five minutes. Lucía reported mild jaundice treated with phototherapy for two days; otherwise the neonatal course was unremarkable, and Mateo was discharged home with his mother on day three.

Mateo's developmental history is notable for three documented episodes of acute otitis media between 8 months and 22 months of age, treated with antibiotics each time. He passed his newborn hearing screening and has not had a formal audiological evaluation since. His pediatrician, Dr. Anand, referred him for tympanometry in June 2026; results showed normal middle ear function bilaterally at that time. Lucía reported no history of seizures, head injury, or hospitalization beyond the neonatal stay. Mateo takes no regular medications. His current working diagnosis from Dr. Anand's office, listed on the referral, is ICD-10 F80.2 (mixed receptive-expressive language disorder, rule out), and he is followed for ICD-10 H65.9 (unspecified nonsuppurative otitis media, resolved).

Motor milestones were within typical limits: Mateo walked independently at 13 months and currently runs, climbs, and uses stairs without support. His physical therapist, James Okafor, PT, DPT, who saw him briefly for toe-walking at age two, discharged him from PT services in March 2025 after he met all gross motor goals. Mateo is also followed intermittently by occupational therapist Megan Whitfield, OTR/L, for mild sensory sensitivities around food textures; Whitfield's most recent note, shared with this office with consent, described Mateo as "a cautious but motivated eater who is expanding his diet slowly."

Family and Language History

Mateo lives with his mother, Lucía Flores-Martínez; his father, Andrés de la Cruz; his older sister, Valentina, age 7; and his infant brother, Diego, age 9 months. The family moved to Greensboro from Reidsville in 2022 and currently rents a home on Winterhaven Drive in Guilford County. Mateo's maternal grandmother, Rosa Martínez, whom the family calls "abuela Rosa," lives nearby and provides child care three afternoons a week while Lucía works. The family's dog, a terrier mix named Max, is frequently mentioned by Mateo and appears to be a strong motivator for him during play-based tasks.

Lucía Flores-Martínez immigrated from Mexico as a teenager and is a native Spanish speaker; she reports comfortable but not fully fluent English. Andrés de la Cruz was born in North Carolina to Mexican parents and is bilingual, though he reports Spanish as his stronger language for complex topics. Spanish is the dominant language spoken in the home among adults; both parents report code-switching with the children, particularly Andrés, who often uses English words and short phrases with Mateo and Valentina. Valentina is reported to be fluent and age-appropriate in both languages and serves informally as a language model and interpreter for Mateo at home, which Lucía says sometimes "lets him get away with pointing instead of talking."

Lucía works part-time at Carolina Poultry Processing LLC, and Andrés works full-time as a technician at Precision Auto Body. The family receives support from several community agencies. They are enrolled with WIC for nutrition support, and Lucía described this program as very helpful when Mateo was an infant. The family was also connected by their service coordinator, Teresa Hinojosa, to the Guilford County Department of Social Services (DSS) for help with their housing application, and more recently to the Guilford County Partnership for Children for a childcare subsidy. A caseworker at a statewide resource agency, the Centro de Recursos y Apoyo para Familias Latinas de Carolina del Norte (CRAFLCN), helped the family complete paperwork for Mateo's Medicaid renewal earlier this year; Lucía said she still calls CRAFLCN whenever she has questions about benefits, and that the staff there always answer in Spanish.

Educational History

Mateo has attended the Sunrise Early Head Start Center on Phillips Avenue in Greensboro since August 2025, four days a week. His classroom teacher, Ms. Patel, reports that Mateo is social and affectionate with adults but has fewer spontaneous interactions with peers than expected for his age; she described him often playing alongside, rather than with, classmates such as Liam and Sofia, and relying on gestures when he wants a turn with a toy. Ms. Patel also noted that Mateo enjoys circle time songs and will attempt to sing along with approximated words.

Mateo's case was opened with the Guilford County CDSA office in July 2026 following the pediatrician's referral. His first IFSP meeting is scheduled for October 20, 2026, pending the results of this evaluation and a concurrent developmental assessment. Teresa Hinojosa has been the family's point of contact throughout this process and attended a portion of the family interview by phone with the family's permission.

ASSESSMENT PROCEDURES

Assessment included parent interview (conducted in Spanish with Sandra Núñez interpreting), review of records from Dr. Anand's office, the Guilford County CDSA office, and Sunrise Early Head Start Center, standardized testing in both English and Spanish, informal language sampling, oral mechanism examination, and clinical observation across both sessions. Standardized tools administered were the Preschool Language Scale, Fifth Edition, Spanish-English Bilingual Edition (PLS-5) and the Goldman-Fristoe Test of Articulation, Third Edition (GFTA-3), administered in English given that the GFTA-3 does not have a validated Spanish norm set; articulation in Spanish was assessed informally through conversational sampling and a Spanish single-word naming task. Dynamic assessment procedures, including mediated learning and test-teach-retest tasks, were used to help distinguish language difference from language disorder, consistent with best practice for bilingual children being evaluated for the first time.

TEST RESULTS

Mateo was cooperative and engaged across both sessions, though he required frequent redirection to task and benefited from short breaks with preferred toys, including a small plush dog he associated with his own pet, Max. Rapport was established quickly, in part because Sandra Núñez greeted him in Spanish and used familiar routines from his home language. Behavioral observations are considered representative of Mateo's typical functioning.

Standardized Test Results

Test / Subtest | Standard Score | 95% CI | Percentile | Age Equivalent
PLS-5 Auditory Comprehension (English) | 73 | 68–78 | 4th | 2;4–2;7
PLS-5 Expressive Communication (English) | 70 | 65–75 | 2nd | 2;1–2;5
PLS-5 Total Language Score (English) | 71 | 67–75 | 3rd | 2;2–2;6
PLS-5 Auditory Comprehension (Spanish) | 79 | 74–84 | 8th | 2;7–2;11
PLS-5 Expressive Communication (Spanish) | 76 | 71–81 | 5th | 2;5–2;9
GFTA-3 Sounds-in-Words (English) | 65 | 59–71 | 1st | 2;0–2;3

Mateo's composite scores on the PLS-5 were higher in Spanish than in English across both the receptive and expressive domains, though both languages fell well below age expectations, which is an important pattern suggesting a true language disorder rather than a difference attributable only to differing exposure. His Total Language Score of 71 in English placed him in the 3rd percentile, more than two standard deviations below the mean, with a 95% confidence interval of 67–75. In Spanish, his combined receptive-expressive performance, calculated informally from subtest raw scores given the lack of a combined Spanish composite in this edition, fell at approximately the 6th percentile for his age, age equivalent range 2;5–2;10.

On the GFTA-3, administered in English, Mateo obtained a standard score of 65 (1st percentile, 95% CI 59–71), reflecting a significant speech sound disorder. Error patterns included consistent fronting of velars (for example, "tat" for the target word "cat," substituting /t/ for /k/), stopping of fricatives (" tho" for "so"), and final consonant deletion (" kuh" for "cup"). Intelligibility in connected speech was estimated at 40% in English for familiar listeners and well under 25% for unfamiliar listeners.

Informal Spanish articulation sampling revealed similar patterns, including stopping of the fricative /s/ and simplification of consonant clusters, as in his production of "teso" for the target "queso" (cheese), again substituting [t] for the velar [k]. He produced the trilled /r/ inconsistently, often realizing it as a flap [ɾ] or omitting it, as in "ato" for "carro" (car). These error patterns were consistent across both languages, which supports a diagnosis of a speech sound disorder affecting both of Mateo's languages rather than a pattern limited to second-language acquisition.

Language sample analysis, coded using standard SALT conventions, showed a mean length of utterance of 2.3 morphemes in English and 2.6 morphemes in Spanish, both below expected ranges for his age in either language. Several utterances were coded [EW] for word-finding difficulty or false starts, for example when Mateo attempted to describe a picture of a birthday party and produced "the... the... um" before his mother supplied the word "pastel" (cake). On a receptive vocabulary probe using familiar household items, he correctly identified 8 of 10 items in Spanish and 6 of 10 in English, a ratio consistent with his reported home language exposure.

Oral mechanism examination was within normal limits for structure and function; no concerns were noted regarding lip, tongue, or palate structure, and diadochokinetic rates were judged age-appropriate, though imprecise. Hearing was not formally retested at this visit, and given his history of recurrent otitis media, a follow-up audiological evaluation is recommended as outlined below.

CLINICAL IMPRESSIONS

Based on standardized testing in both of Mateo's languages, parent report, classroom observation reported by Ms. Patel, and informal dynamic assessment, Mateo presents with a speech sound disorder and an expressive-receptive language disorder affecting both Spanish and English. His performance pattern, with below-average scores in both languages that show the same phonological error patterns across languages, supports a true disorder rather than a language difference secondary to dual language exposure or limited English proficiency. This distinction is clinically important: had Mateo shown strong skills in Spanish with only weak English, a pattern consistent with typical second-language acquisition would be more likely, and services would not be indicated on that basis alone.

Mateo's combination of reduced intelligibility, limited phonemic inventory (consistent deletion of final consonants, fronting of velars such as /k/ and /g/, and stopping of fricatives including /s/ and /f/), and below-average expressive and receptive language scores in both languages meets criteria for eligibility for Part C early intervention services under North Carolina's established eligibility guidelines, which this examiner understands to require a 25% delay or a score at least 1.5 standard deviations below the mean in one or more developmental domains. Mateo meets this threshold in both speech sound production and expressive language, and is borderline in receptive language.

Mateo's family and community supports, including involvement with WIC, the Guilford County Partnership for Children, DSS, and CRAFLCN, along with his parents' consistent engagement in this evaluation process, are considered strong protective factors that should support his response to intervention.

RECOMMENDATIONS

1. Mateo is recommended for bilingual speech-language therapy services through Part C early intervention, to be coordinated with his service coordinator, Teresa Hinojosa, and incorporated into IFSP Outcome 1 and IFSP Outcome 2 at his upcoming meeting on October 20, 2026.

2. Therapy should address speech sound production in both Spanish and English concurrently, using a cycles phonological approach (Cycles) targeting velar fronting, final consonant deletion, and stopping of fricatives, with cueing progressing from max cues to min cues as accuracy improves.

3. Expressive and receptive language goals should use a combination of Hanen-based parent coaching strategies and structured vocabulary expansion activities, delivered primarily in Spanish with English modeling as appropriate, to build Mateo's language foundation in his dominant home language while supporting continued English exposure at Sunrise Early Head Start Center.

4. A follow-up audiological evaluation is recommended given Mateo's history of recurrent otitis media, to rule out any fluctuating conductive hearing loss contributing to his speech and language delays. This can be coordinated through Dr. Anand's office.

5. Continued occupational therapy consultation with Megan Whitfield is recommended to monitor feeding-related sensory sensitivities, as reduced oral exploration of varied textures may have secondary effects on articulatory development.

6. Parent coaching sessions should include both Lucía Flores-Martínez and Andrés de la Cruz when possible, with interpretation support from Sandra Núñez or another qualified interpreter, to ensure both parents can implement home strategies confidently in their stronger language.

7. Mateo's classroom teacher, Ms. Patel, should be provided with a simple home-school communication log and basic peer-facilitation strategies to increase Mateo's spontaneous verbal interaction with classmates such as Liam and Sofia during structured play.

8. This evaluation should be shared with the Guilford County CDSA office to support eligibility determination and IFSP development, and with DSS and CRAFLCN as needed to assist the family with any related benefit or service coordination questions.

9. Re-evaluation is recommended in 6 months to monitor progress in both languages and to reassess the need for continued dual-language versus single-language service delivery as Mateo's profile develops.

Billing codes for this evaluation: CPT 92523 (evaluation of speech sound production with evaluation of language comprehension and expression), modifier GN.

This report reflects Mateo's skills as observed during this evaluation and should be considered alongside ongoing observation from family, providers, and Sunrise Early Head Start Center staff. Please contact this office with any questions.

Respectfully submitted,

Rachel Boyd, M.S., CCC-SLP
Bilingual-Certified Speech-Language Pathologist
Piedmont Bilingual Speech & Language Associates, PLLC

SPEECH-LANGUAGE EVALUATION REPORT

Date of Report: September 18, 2026
Dates of Evaluation: September 9, 2026 and September 11, 2026

Child's Name: Mateo Alejandro Hernández Cruz (called "Teo" at home and "Mateo" at school)
Date of Birth: July 3, 2022
Chronological Age at Evaluation: 4;2
Gender: Male
Primary Language(s): Spanish and English (bilingual home)

Service Coordinator: Michelle Davis

Sibling: Camila Hernández (age 7)
Other household members: maternal grandmother Rosa Cruz, who provides after-school care
Family pet: a dog named Rocky

School/Daycare: Mateo attends pre-kindergarten at Jesse Wharton Elementary School in Guilford County Schools, in Ms. Amanda Lopez's classroom.

Interpreter Services: Spanish-English interpretation was provided by Ana Torres, a certified medical interpreter, for all parent interview portions of this evaluation.

Referral Source: Pediatrician Dr. Sarah Kim of Lindley Park Pediatrics referred the family for a comprehensive speech-language evaluation due to concerns about limited expressive vocabulary and unintelligible speech in both languages.

Evaluating Clinician: Maria Gonzalez, M.S., CCC-SLP, bilingual pediatric speech-language pathologist

REASON FOR REFERRAL

Teo is a 4;2-year-old boy referred for a bilingual speech-language evaluation following concerns raised by his mother, Lucía Rodríguez, and his teacher, Ms. Amanda Lopez, regarding delayed expressive language and reduced speech intelligibility in Spanish and English. Lucía Rodríguez reported that Teo frequently points or gestures to communicate and becomes frustrated when he is not understood, sometimes during drop-off at 7:45 a.m. and pickup at 3:15 p.m.. Ms. Amanda Lopez noted during a phone consultation on August 28, 2026 that Teo struggles to follow multi-step directions during circle time, which occurs daily at 9:00 a.m., and that his peers, including his classmate Diego Martínez, often repeat or rephrase his requests for him.

BACKGROUND INFORMATION

Background information was obtained through parent interview (conducted in Spanish with interpretation by Ana Torres), review of prior records from Piedmont Triad Children's Developmental Services Agency, a classroom observation at Jesse Wharton Elementary School, and direct assessment of Teo across two sessions.

BIRTH AND MEDICAL HISTORY

Lucía Rodríguez reported an uncomplicated pregnancy with regular prenatal care through Cone Health Women's Hospital. Teo was born at 39 weeks gestational age via vaginal delivery, with a birth weight of 7 lbs 4 oz and Apgar scores of 8 at one minute and 9 at five minutes. There were no complications during the neonatal period, and Teo was discharged home with his mother after a standard two-day hospital stay at Cone Health Women's Hospital.

Medical history is significant for recurrent otitis media, with 4 documented episodes between 12 and 24 months of age, treated with antibiotics by his pediatrician, Dr. Sarah Kim. Tympanostomy tubes were placed on May 14, 2024 by Dr. Robert Chen, an otolaryngologist at Triad ENT Associates. Hearing was last screened on June 2, 2026 and results were within normal limits bilaterally. No history of seizures, significant head injury, or hospitalization beyond birth was reported. Teo is not currently on any medications. His most recent well-child visit with Dr. Sarah Kim occurred on August 15, 2026.

Teo receives occupational therapy and physical therapy services through Piedmont Triad Children's Developmental Services Agency. His occupational therapist, Jennifer Walsh, reported mild fine motor delays affecting pencil grasp and buttoning, and his physical therapist, Carlos Mendoza, noted age-appropriate gross motor skills with intervention focused on coordination during group games. Both providers see Teo weekly, with occupational therapy sessions typically held on Tuesday mornings beginning at 10:30 a.m. and physical therapy sessions on Thursday afternoons beginning at 1:00 p.m..

FAMILY AND LANGUAGE HISTORY

Teo lives with his mother, Lucía Rodríguez, his father, Francisco Hernández, and his older sister, Camila Hernández, at 1142 Willow Oak Drive, Greensboro, 27403. His maternal grandmother, Rosa Cruz, lives nearby and cares for Teo and Camila Hernández after school several days per week while Lucía Rodríguez works at Biscuitville Corporate Office and Francisco Hernández works in construction.

Spanish is the primary language spoken in the home. Lucía Rodríguez reported that she and Francisco Hernández speak almost exclusively Spanish with Teo and Camila Hernández, while Rosa Cruz speaks only Spanish. Teo has been exposed to English primarily through pre-kindergarten, which he began attending at age 3;8. Lucía Rodríguez described Teo as using single words and short phrases in Spanish at home, such as "quiero agua" and "más," but rarely combining more than two or three words. She reported that extended family, including Teo's paternal uncle Jesús Hernández, called affectionately "Chuy," have also expressed concern about his limited verbal output during family gatherings.

Lucía Rodríguez denied any family history of speech, language, or learning disabilities on her side, but noted that Francisco Hernández's brother, whom the family calls "Pepe," had a speech delay as a child and received therapy services. Teo's sister, Camila Hernández, is reported to have typical language development and often translates or speaks on her brother's behalf.

DEVELOPMENTAL HISTORY

Lucía Rodríguez reported that Teo sat independently at approximately 7 months, walked at 14 months, and said his first word, "mamá," at approximately 16 months. She described his vocabulary growth as notably slower than his sister's at the same age. Teo began combining two words at approximately 30 months, later than typical milestones for either language. Social and play skills were described as age-appropriate; Teo engages in pretend play with toy cars and enjoys playing with his cousin Juanito and neighborhood friend Lupita during weekend visits.

ASSESSMENT PROCEDURES

The evaluation was conducted across two sessions at the offices of Carolina Bilingual Speech & Language Services, PLLC. The first session began at 9:15 a.m. and concluded at 11:30 a.m. on September 9, 2026, and included parent interview, hearing screening review, and administration of standardized assessments in Spanish. The second session began at 1:45 p.m. and concluded at 3:30 p.m. on September 11, 2026, and included administration of standardized assessments in English, an oral-motor examination, and a language sample. Ana Torres provided interpretation during the parent interview portion only; all direct testing with Teo was conducted by Maria Gonzalez, who is a native Spanish speaker and bilingual service provider.

The following standardized and informal measures were administered:

- Preschool Language Scales, Fifth Edition, Spanish (PLS-5 Spanish)
- Clinical Evaluation of Language Fundamentals, Fifth Edition (CELF-5)
- Goldman-Fristoe Test of Articulation, Third Edition (GFTA-3)
- Bilingual English Spanish Assessment (BESA), Morphosyntax subtest
- Oral-motor examination
- Spontaneous language sample (Spanish and English, 50 utterances each)
- Parent interview and case history review
- Classroom observation at Jesse Wharton Elementary School

TEST RESULTS

Teo presented as a cooperative, friendly child who engaged readily with testing materials in both languages. Standardized scores are summarized below. Given Teo's bilingual exposure, Spanish-language measures are considered most representative of his underlying language ability, while English measures reflect his developing second-language skills.

Test/Subtest	Standard Score	Percentile Rank	Age Equivalent	Classification
PLS-5 Spanish Auditory Comprehension	78	7th	2;9–3;0	Below Average
PLS-5 Spanish Expressive Communication	71	3rd	2;6–2;9	Below Average
PLS-5 Spanish Total Language Score	73	4th	2;8–3;0	Below Average
CELF-5 Core Language Score	65	1st	2;3–2;6	Well Below Average
CELF-5 Receptive Language Index	70	2nd	2;6–2;9	Below Average
GFTA-3 Sounds-in-Words	76	6th	3;0–3;3	Below Average
BESA Morphosyntax Index	68	2nd	Not calculated	Below Average

PLS-5 Spanish composite scores fell within the range of 65-80 across subtests, consistent with a significant delay relative to same-age Spanish-speaking peers. CELF-5 scores in English, administered to estimate second-language functioning, fell within the range of 60-72, as expected given Teo's limited exposure to English prior to pre-kindergarten enrollment. The discrepancy between his Spanish and English scores is consistent with typical second-language acquisition patterns rather than indicating two separate disorders; however, the delay observed in his dominant language, Spanish, is clinically significant and indicative of a true language impairment.

Articulation testing on the GFTA-3 revealed sound errors including final consonant deletion (e.g., "cat" produced as "ca"), cluster reduction (e.g., "star" produced as "tar"), and substitution of /k/ for /t/ in word-initial position. In Spanish, similar patterns were observed, with /r/ frequently produced as [w] and liquids such as /ɾ/ distorted in words like "pero," produced as "peo." Overall speech intelligibility was estimated at approximately 60% in context for unfamiliar listeners and 80% for familiar listeners such as Lucía Rodríguez and Rosa Cruz.

Oral-motor examination revealed structures and function within normal limits for speech; no evidence of apraxia or dysarthria was noted. Diadochokinetic rates were judged age-appropriate.

During the spontaneous language sample, Teo produced primarily single-word and two-word utterances in both languages, with occasional three-word combinations in Spanish (e.g., "quiero más agua"). Mean length of utterance in Spanish was calculated at 2.1 morphemes, and in English at 1.6 morphemes, both below expectations for his age. SALT coding identified frequent use of [EW] codes for word-finding difficulty and omission of grammatical morphemes, particularly plural "-s" and articles in both languages.

During cueing tasks, Teo required moderate cues (mod cues) to produce target vocabulary items and minimal cues (min cues) to imitate simple two-word phrases. He achieved 6 of 10 correct productions of target words with moderate visual and verbal cueing, improving to 8/10 with repeated trials.

CLASSROOM OBSERVATION

A classroom observation was conducted at Jesse Wharton Elementary School on September 10, 2026 during morning circle time, which began at 9:00 a.m.. Teo was observed in Ms. Amanda Lopez's classroom, where he participated in a song-based activity but did not initiate verbal responses when called on. His classmate Diego Martínez was observed answering on Teo's behalf when Teo hesitated. Teaching assistant Mr. David Alvarez was noted to provide frequent visual supports and gestural cues to support Teo's comprehension of classroom directions. During free play from 9:45 a.m. to 10:15 a.m., Teo engaged in parallel play with blocks alongside peers but used minimal verbal communication, relying primarily on gesture and gaze to request materials.

IMPRESSIONS

Teo presents with a primary language impairment affecting both receptive and expressive language skills in his dominant language, Spanish, as well as delayed second-language (English) development consistent with limited exposure. His performance across standardized Spanish measures, including the PLS-5 Spanish and BESA, falls within the below-average to well-below-average range, indicating a true language disorder rather than typical second-language acquisition alone. Articulation errors in both languages further reduce overall speech intelligibility, impacting his ability to communicate effectively with unfamiliar listeners, including teachers and peers at Jesse Wharton Elementary School.

Given the consistency of delays across both languages in morphosyntax, vocabulary, and sound production, in combination with history of recurrent otitis media and normal current hearing status confirmed by audiologic screening, Teo meets criteria for a mixed receptive-expressive language disorder (ICD-10 code F80.2) with concomitant phonological disorder (ICD-10 code F80.0). These findings support continued eligibility for early intervention services through Piedmont Triad Children's Developmental Services Agency and warrant consideration of continued speech-language therapy services as he transitions into the public school system through Guilford County Schools.

Teo's strengths include strong nonverbal communication skills, good eye contact, appropriate social engagement with peers and family members, and a cooperative, motivated disposition during structured testing tasks. He benefits from visual supports, moderate cueing, and bilingual input, all of which should be incorporated into intervention planning.

RECOMMENDATIONS

1. Teo should continue to receive speech-language therapy services, ideally delivered bilingually or in close coordination with a bilingual provider, at a frequency of two sessions per week, 30 minutes each, focusing on expressive vocabulary growth, sentence structure, and speech sound production in both Spanish and English.

2. Treatment approaches should include Hanen-based strategies to support parent coaching and naturalistic language facilitation in the home, given the family's strong desire to maintain Spanish as the primary home language. PROMPT techniques are recommended to address tactile-kinesthetic cueing for articulation targets, and a Cycles approach is recommended to address phonological patterns including final consonant deletion and cluster reduction.

3. Coordination with occupational therapist Jennifer Walsh and physical therapist Carlos Mendoza is recommended to ensure consistency of cueing strategies across disciplines and to support generalization of communication goals during motor-based activities.

4. Continued coordination with pediatrician Dr. Sarah Kim is recommended to monitor for any recurrence of otitis media, given the known association between chronic middle ear fluid and speech-language delay.

5. School-based consultation with Ms. Amanda Lopez and teaching assistant Mr. David Alvarez is recommended to implement classroom strategies such as pre-teaching vocabulary, allowing additional response time, and using visual schedules to support comprehension of multi-step directions.

6. Family training sessions with Lucía Rodríguez and Francisco Hernández, supported by interpreter services as needed, are recommended to teach specific language facilitation strategies for use during daily routines, including mealtimes and bedtime.

7. Re-evaluation is recommended in approximately six months, or sooner if significant progress or concerns arise, to update standardized scores and adjust the treatment plan accordingly.

8. The family should be connected with Smart Start of Guilford County for information regarding additional community-based language enrichment programs, and the service coordinator, Michelle Davis, should assist with transition planning as Teo approaches his third birthday relative to Part C to Part B transition under IDEA.

This report reflects Teo's skills as observed during the dates of evaluation listed above and should be considered alongside ongoing clinical observation and input from family and other providers.

Respectfully submitted,

Maria Gonzalez, M.S., CCC-SLP
