Piedmont Pediatric Speech & Language Clinic
2140 Westover Terrace, Suite 310
Greensboro, NC 27408
Phone: (336) 555-0148 | Fax: (336) 555-0149
Website: www.piedmontspeechkids.com

October 2, 2026

RE: Speech-Language Evaluation
Child: Mateo Alejandro Flores
Date of Birth: April 14, 2022
Chronological Age at Evaluation: 4;5
Medicaid ID: 887234561B
CDSA Case Number: CDSA-NC-2026-05193
Evaluation Date: September 29, 2026

Dear Lucía Flores Ramírez and Ricardo Flores,

Thank you for bringing Mateo in to see me on September 29, 2026. I know evaluations can feel overwhelming, so I want to walk you through what we did, what we found, and what we think will help Mateo the most. This letter will go in his file at the Agencia de Servicios para el Desarrollo Infantil Temprano del Piedmont Central (the CDSA Piedmont Central) and will also be shared with his service coordinator at the Agencia de Coordinación de Servicios Familiares del Condado de Alamance (the Coordinación Familiar de Alamance) so that his team can plan next steps together.

My name is Ashley Whitfield, M.S., CCC-SLP, and I am bilingual in English and Spanish. I met with Mateo, both of you, and your interpreter, Sandra Peña, for about two hours at our Greensboro office. I also spoke by phone beforehand with Mateo's pediatrician, Dr. Ifeoma Okafor, and with his current teacher at Tiny Acorns Clubhouse, Ms. Hannah Reyes, to get a full picture of how he communicates across settings.

BACKGROUND

You told me that you first became worried about Mateo's talking around his second birthday, when he was not yet combining words the way his older sister, Camila, had at that age. Camila is now 7 years old and in second grade, and you mentioned that she sometimes "translates" for Mateo when he gets frustrated. Mateo was referred to the CDSA by Ms. Reyes after she noticed that he mostly points and uses single words in class, while classmates like Liam and Daniela are already using full sentences.

Mateo has been enrolled at Tiny Acorns Clubhouse on Alamance Road since January 2025. You explained that his grandmother, Rosa Ramírez, picked him up most afternoons until this past summer, when she moved back to be closer to extended family. Since then, Mateo's godmother, Dolores Navarro, has helped with pickup two days a week.

BIRTH AND MEDICAL HISTORY

Lucía Flores Ramírez reported an uncomplicated pregnancy with Mateo. He was born at 39 weeks gestation by vaginal delivery, weighing 7 lbs 2 oz, with Apgar scores of 8 and 9. There were no NICU stays and no feeding concerns in infancy. Mateo met his gross motor milestones close to on time (walking around 13 months) but his first words did not emerge until closer to 20 months, and word combinations have been slow to develop since.

Mateo passed his newborn hearing screening and had a repeat audiological evaluation on June 11, 2026, which showed normal hearing bilaterally. He has had four documented episodes of otitis media, most recently in February 2026, treated with antibiotics by Dr. Okafor; tubes have not been placed. His last well-child visit was August 3, 2026, at which point Dr. Okafor noted no other medical concerns and supported this referral, documenting it under ICD-10 code F80.1 (expressive language disorder, rule out) in his chart.

There is no family history of autism. You did mention that Mateo's uncle, Héctor Flores, was described as a "late talker" as a child but spoke clearly by first grade.

FAMILY AND LANGUAGE HISTORY

Your home is a wonderful bilingual environment. Lucía speaks mostly Spanish with Mateo, while Ricardo uses both English and Spanish depending on the activity. Camila speaks English at school and switches between both languages at home, and she often narrates for Mateo when he is quiet with new people. You estimate Mateo hears Spanish about 60 percent of the time and English about 40 percent of the time across his week, largely because of his hours at Tiny Acorns Clubhouse, where instruction is in English.

You both moved to North Carolina from El Rosario, a small village outside Choluteca, Honduras, in 2019, before Mateo was born. Lucía's mother, Rosa Ramírez, still lives part of the year in El Rosario and part of the year with your family at your current home at 118 Winding Creek Court, Burlington, NC 27217. Ricardo works days in construction, and Lucía works nights at the Carolina Fresh Poultry Processing Plant, which is why appointments earlier than 4:00 p.m. are hard for your family to attend; we appreciated your flexibility in coming in at 1:30 p.m. today.

The family dog, Rocky, is apparently Mateo's favorite "listener," and you shared that he will sit and "talk" to Rocky in long strings of jargon that are hard for adults to interpret, saying things like "Rocky no" and "upa Rocky" when he wants to be picked up alongside the dog.

ASSESSMENT PROCEDURES

I administered standardized testing in both English and Spanish, used informal observation and play-based sampling, and reviewed the records you and Dr. Okafor's office provided. Mateo was cooperative throughout, though he needed frequent breaks and responded best to concrete, high-interest toys (cars, animal figures, and bubbles). Ms. Peña interpreted all Spanish-language instructions and conversation with the family, and I directly administered the English-language test items myself, since I am fluent in both languages.

Tests administered included the Preschool Language Scales, Fifth Edition (PLS-5) in both English and Spanish forms, the Goldman-Fristoe Test of Articulation, Third Edition (GFTA-3), an oral mechanism examination, and a 20-minute play-based language sample. CPT code 92523 was used for the combined evaluation of speech sound production and language comprehension and expression.

TEST RESULTS

PLS-5 (English Form):

| Subtest | Standard Score | Percentile Rank | Confidence Interval |
|---|---|---|---|
| Auditory Comprehension | 78 | 7th | 70-86 |
| Expressive Communication | 65 | 1st | 57-73 |
| Total Language Score | 69 | 2nd | 61-77 |

PLS-5 (Spanish Form):

| Subtest | Standard Score | Percentile Rank | Confidence Interval |
|---|---|---|---|
| Auditory Comprehension | 81 | 10th | 73-89 |
| Expressive Communication | 70 | 2nd | 62-78 |
| Total Language Score | 74 | 4th | 66-82 |

Mateo's best performance in each domain, taken together across both languages (conceptual scoring), suggests Auditory Comprehension in the low average range and Expressive Communication falling in the moderately delayed range for his age. His combined age equivalent for expressive language was 2;4, notably below his chronological age of 4;5.

GFTA-3 (English, administered alongside Spanish phonological screening):

| Measure | Standard Score | Percentile Rank |
|---|---|---|
| Sounds-in-Words | 82 | 12th |

Mateo's speech sound errors were largely consistent with normal developmental patterns for his age, with substitution of /θ/ for /s/ and inconsistent production of /ɾ/ in Spanish words, both considered age-appropriate at 4;5. His intelligibility was judged fair, estimated at 60 percent intelligible to unfamiliar listeners in connected speech, improving to 85 percent with context and gesture.

LANGUAGE SAMPLE OBSERVATIONS

During the play-based sample, Mateo's utterances were primarily single words and two-word combinations ("more car," "no quiero," "upa Rocky"). He used approximately 35 different words across the session, well below the 150-plus words typical for his age. His Mean Length of Utterance was 1.6 morphemes. He imitated the target phrase "quiero jugo" with moderate cues, producing "quio jugo," which showed appropriate attempt at the full phrase structure. He used gestures and pointing to supplement roughly 40 percent of his communicative attempts, which is a helpful compensatory strategy but also a sign that verbal language is not yet carrying the communicative load it should at his age.

I also noted that Mateo followed simple, one-step directions reliably (8 of 10 in English, 9/10 in Spanish) but struggled with two-step directions without gestural support (3 of 10 in both languages). His joint attention and eye contact were age-appropriate, and he showed clear social reciprocity, smiling, taking turns in simple games, and seeking out adult attention to share enjoyment, which is reassuring and argues against a broader social communication disorder.

ORAL MECHANISM EXAMINATION

Structure and function of the oral mechanism were within normal limits. No signs of dysarthria, apraxia red flags, or structural abnormality were noted. Diadochokinetic rates were age-appropriate.

IMPRESSIONS

Based on today's assessment, parent and teacher report, and medical history, Mateo presents with a Developmental Language Disorder, with expressive language more significantly affected than receptive language, in both of his languages. This is not simply a function of learning two languages; his delays are present and comparable in both English and Spanish, which tells us this is a true language-learning difficulty rather than typical bilingual development. His speech sound production is age-appropriate once accounting for normal bilingual phonological patterns, and his social communication skills (joint attention, reciprocity, play) are a relative strength and do not raise concern for autism spectrum disorder at this time.

Mateo's history of recurrent ear infections may have contributed to some early language-learning difficulty, but his current hearing is normal, so ongoing speech-language intervention, not medical treatment, is the right next step.

RECOMMENDATIONS

1. Mateo qualifies for ongoing speech-language intervention services through his IFSP. I recommend Outcome 2 be updated to target functional, multi-word expressive language in both English and Spanish.

2. Direct speech-language therapy, twice weekly for 30-minute sessions, focused on expanding utterance length, increasing vocabulary diversity, and building two-word and three-word combinations. I recommend a Hanen-informed, parent-coaching approach (the "It Takes Two to Talk" model) so that both of you can use the same strategies at home and so Camila is not carrying the "interpreter" role for her brother.

3. Continued bilingual language exposure at home. Please do not reduce Spanish input in an effort to "help" English develop faster; children build strongest overall language skills when both languages are supported, and Mateo's pattern of comparable delay in both languages confirms this is a language disorder, not a bilingualism issue.

4. Classroom supports at Tiny Acorns Clubhouse: I will send Ms. Reyes a one-page strategy sheet with sentence-expansion techniques (for example, expanding "more car" to "I want more car, please") and suggestions for incorporating more peer-modeling opportunities with classmates like Liam, who is a strong verbal model.

5. Re-screening of hearing in 6 months given his history of recurrent otitis media, coordinated with Dr. Okafor.

6. Family training session with Sandra Peña interpreting, scheduled for October 20, 2026 at 5:30 p.m., to review home strategies in detail.

7. Reassessment in approximately 6 months to monitor progress and adjust IFSP outcomes as needed, ideally timed with his annual review on March 15, 2027.

NEXT STEPS

Your service coordinator at Coordinación Familiar de Alamance, Denise Walker, will be reaching out this week to schedule the IFSP review meeting. If you have questions before then, you can reach our office directly, or you can email me at awhitfield@piedmontspeechkids.com. Our front desk can also be reached at (336) 555-0148 if scheduling works better by phone.

I know this is a lot of information, and I want you to know that Mateo is a bright, affectionate little boy who clearly loves his family, his sister, and even his dog Rocky very much. With consistent support in both languages, children with this profile typically make strong progress. We are glad to be part of his team.

Please do not hesitate to reach out with any questions.

Warm regards,

Ashley Whitfield, M.S., CCC-SLP
Piedmont Pediatric Speech & Language Clinic
(336) 555-0148
awhitfield@piedmontspeechkids.com

Hi Lucía and Brenda,

Pasting the final report below for your records, and copying Diego since he asked to be looped in. Let me know if the CDSA file needs anything reformatted before the October 23, 2026 IFSP review.

---

**Piedmont Bilingual Speech & Language Services, PLLC**
Speech-Language Evaluation Report

Client: Mateo Hernández Cruz ("M.H.C.")
Date of Birth: February 14, 2023
Chronological Age at Evaluation: 3;8
Evaluation Dates: October 1, 2026 and October 3, 2026
Report Date: October 9, 2026
Medicaid ID: 748203915K
Record Number: PCDSA-22948
Referral Source: Piedmont CDSA, Service Coordinator Brenda Alvarez
Evaluator: Mara Jennings, M.S., CCC-SLP, Bilingual (English/Spanish)
Interpreter: Not required; evaluator is bilingual
Address: 214 Bentgrass Lane, Mebane, NC 27302
Home Phone: (336) 555-0142
Parent Email: lucia.rodriguez82@gmail.com

**Reason for Referral**

Mateo was referred by Piedmont CDSA for a comprehensive bilingual speech-language evaluation following parent and daycare concern regarding limited intelligibility in both English and Spanish, reduced expressive vocabulary relative to peers, and difficulty following multi-step directions. His mother, Lucía Rodríguez Fernández, and his father, Diego Hernández Morales, completed intake forms in Spanish and English respectively. Mateo currently attends Little Sprouts Bilingual Daycare four days a week, where his lead teacher, Ms. Patel, first raised concerns at his 3;6 developmental checkpoint.

**Background and Developmental History**

Mateo is the younger of two children born to Lucía and Diego. His older sister, Sol Hernández Cruz, is seven years old and attends second grade. Sol has no known developmental concerns and is reportedly a frequent play partner and interpreter-by-proxy for Mateo at home, often repeating his utterances for other family members. The family also has a dog, Max, whom Mateo is reported to call often by name.

Mateo was born at 37 weeks gestational age at Alamance Regional Medical Center in Burlington, NC, via scheduled cesarean section due to breech presentation. Birth weight was 5 lb 9 oz and Apgar scores were 7 and 9 at one and five minutes. He was admitted to the Alamance Regional Medical Center NICU for four days for monitoring of mild respiratory distress and transient hypoglycemia; his attending neonatologist there was Dr. Patricia Nwosu. He has since been followed by his pediatrician, Dr. Samuel Okafor, for routine well-child care, and was referred at 2;10 to an ENT, Dr. Grace Thompson, for recurrent otitis media; he had bilateral myringotomy tubes placed at 3;0, with resolution of middle ear effusion confirmed at his most recent follow-up.

Parents report no other significant medical history. Mateo passed his newborn hearing screening and a repeat audiological evaluation at 3;1 showed normal hearing bilaterally. Motor and self-help milestones were within normal limits per parent report (walked at 13 months, fed self with a spoon by 18 months).

**Family, Language, and Early Intervention History**

The family is bilingual, with Spanish spoken predominantly in the home and English introduced through daycare and extended family contact. Lucía grew up in La Esperanza, a small village outside Comayagua, Honduras, and moved to the United States when Mateo was 18 months old. Prior to immigrating, Mateo received brief early-intervention screening services in Honduras through the Centro de Apoyo y Desarrollo Integral para la Niñez y la Familia (CADINF), a regional nonprofit serving children with developmental delays across several departments. Records transferred by Lucía indicate that CADINF staff noted "delayed babbling" at 11 months but did not recommend formal services at that time given the family's planned relocation.

Diego was born and raised in Hillsborough, NC, and reports he did not begin speaking in full sentences until after age three, a history he describes as similar to Mateo's current presentation. Extended family support includes Mateo's maternal grandmother, Rosa Fernández, who provides childcare two afternoons a week and speaks only Spanish with him.

**Assessment Procedures**

The following bilingual measures and informal procedures were administered across two sessions, with portions of session two conducted in the family's home at 4:30 PM to observe naturalistic play-based language use:

- Preschool Language Scales, Fifth Edition, Spanish-Bilingual Edition (PLS-5 Spanish-Bilingual)
- Goldman-Fristoe Test of Articulation, Third Edition (GFTA-3)
- Bilingual English Spanish Assessment (BESA), Morphosyntax Subtest
- Spontaneous language sample (English and Spanish), SALT-coded
- Oral mechanism examination
- Parent interview and Rossetti Infant-Toddler Language Scale caregiver questionnaire (supplemental)

**Test Results**

| Domain | Measure | Admin Date | Standard Score | Percentile | 90% CI |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Auditory Comprehension | PLS-5 Spanish-Bilingual | 10/01/2026 | 82 | 12th | 73-83 |
| Expressive Communication | PLS-5 Spanish-Bilingual | 10/01/2026 | 76 | 5th | 68-84 |
| Total Language Score | PLS-5 Spanish-Bilingual | 10/01/2026 | 78 | 7th | 70-86 |
| Articulation Composite | GFTA-3 | 10/03/2026 | 71 | 3rd | 65-77 |
| Morphosyntax | BESA | 10/03/2026 | 19 (scaled) | 9th | 14-24 |

**Speech Sound Production**

Mateo's speech was approximately 55% intelligible to unfamiliar listeners in connected speech and 75% intelligible to familiar listeners. Phonological processes observed included final consonant deletion, cluster reduction, and gliding of liquids (e.g., /w/ for /r/). On a word-finding and articulation probe using family-salient vocabulary, the target word "sol" (meaning "sun") was elicited five times; Mateo produced it as "tol" in 4 of 5 trials, substituting /t/ for /s/ and showing stable production of the final consonant. This target was selected because it is phonetically similar to several high-frequency words in the home and because it carries personal relevance; it is not a reference to any family member's name. When shown a photo of his sister and asked to label her, Mateo instead said "Sol" clearly and without substitution, suggesting the name itself is a stored whole-word form distinct from his production of the common noun "sol."

In Spanish, cluster reduction was also noted on words such as "flor" produced as "for," and gliding was observed in English on "rabbit" produced as "wabbit." Oral mechanism exam was within normal limits for structure and function; no concerns for dysarthria or apraxia were noted, though a mild reduction in diadochokinetic rate was observed.

**Language Sample Analysis**

A 100-utterance spontaneous language sample was collected across both English and Spanish contexts. Mean length of utterance in morphemes (MLUm) was 2.8 in English and 3.1 in Spanish, both below age expectations (3;8). SALT coding flagged frequent omission of grammatical morphemes, coded as [EW] (error, word-level) and [EO] (error, omission) across both languages. Mateo used primarily two- and three-word utterances, relied on gesture to supplement communication, and showed better performance in structured one-on-one interaction than in group play observed briefly with his daycare classmate Ethan.

**Impressions**

Mateo presents with a bilingual speech sound disorder and expressive-receptive language delay affecting both English and Spanish, consistent with a true language disorder rather than a difference attributable to typical second-language acquisition, given comparable delays across both languages and a positive family history of late language emergence. Relevant ICD-10 code: F80.9 (Developmental disorder of speech and language, unspecified). Relevant CPT codes used for this evaluation: 92523 (evaluation of speech sound production with evaluation of language comprehension and expression) and 92521 (modifier not applicable).

Given his history of recurrent otitis media and recent tube placement, ongoing monitoring of hearing status in coordination with Dr. Grace Thompson is recommended. Family and early-intervention history, including the brief CADINF screening in Honduras, support a developmental rather than purely environmental explanation for his current delays.

**Recommendations**

1. Mateo qualifies for ongoing early intervention services under IFSP Outcome 2 (communication) and IFSP Outcome 3 (social-emotional/play skills), to be reviewed at the October 23, 2026 IFSP meeting.
2. Individual speech-language therapy, bilingual service delivery, 2x/week, 30 minutes per session, focusing on phonological awareness, expressive vocabulary growth, and morphosyntax in both languages.
3. Use of a modified Hanen "It Takes Two to Talk" coaching model with parents to support language stimulation techniques at home in Spanish.
4. Consider a brief trial of PROMPT tactile-kinesthetic cueing for targeted sound classes given reduced intelligibility.
5. Continued ENT follow-up with Dr. Grace Thompson regarding middle ear status.
6. Classroom-based support at Little Sprouts Bilingual Daycare, with Ms. Patel encouraged to use simplified, expanded models of Mateo's utterances rather than corrections.
7. Re-evaluation in 6 months or at IFSP review, whichever comes first.

Thank you for the opportunity to work with this family.

Mara Jennings, M.S., CCC-SLP
Bilingual Speech-Language Pathologist
Piedmont Bilingual Speech & Language Services, PLLC

- Carlos del Río added, "A veces se frustra mucho porque no lo entendemos" (Sometimes he gets very frustrated because we don't understand him).

child: mateo alejandro flores vega
preferred name: mateo

reason for referral

mateo was referred for a comprehensive bilingual speech and language evaluation by dr patricia nguyen at atrium health pediatrics university city after his eighteen month well child check showed limited expressive vocabulary and his mother lucía rodríguez flores reported ongoing concern that he was not combining words the way his older sister sol did at the same age the family learned about this clinic from a friend diana suarez whose own son received services here about two years ago and recommended elena castillo directly the family was also connected with mecklenburg county children's developmental services agency the cdsa office for early intervention service coordination through yesenia ortiz the service coordinator who has been following the family since november 2023 and a brief referral was also made to mecklenburg county smart start for a parenting and language stimulation class which the mother has not yet attended due to her work schedule

birth and medical history

mateo was born on april 9 2022 at atrium health levine children's hospital myers park campus at 35 weeks gestation following a pregnancy complicated by preeclampsia his birth weight was 4 pounds 11 ounces and his apgar scores were 6 and 8 at one and five minutes he spent 19 days in the nicu at the same campus for respiratory support and feeding difficulty and was followed after discharge by dr samuel ahn neonatology his mother reports no other complications during the pregnancy and no family history of hearing loss or speech delay on either side though she notes that her own brother hope ramos did not begin talking until he was almost three and eventually grew out of it without any formal services early motor milestones were mildly delayed with independent walking achieved around 16 months and his pediatrician monitored low muscle tone through his second year though a referral to physical therapy was not pursued because the family felt he was progressing on his own

mateo was seen for an audiological evaluation on march 3 2025 at atrium health ent and audiology ballantyne campus by dr michael sato audiology following parent report of frequent ear infections results showed normal hearing sensitivity bilaterally with type a tympanograms bilaterally and no further audiology follow up was recommended at that time however he has had four documented episodes of otitis media since 2023 and was seen by dr rina patel ent at the same campus who placed bilateral pe tubes on july 14 2024 under general anesthesia cpt code 69436 with no complications a follow up ent visit on january 9 2025 confirmed the tubes were in place and functioning well and middle ear status has remained stable since

family and language history

the family lives at 4821 old pineville road in charlotte in a three bedroom apartment with mateo his parents and his older sister sol who is 7 years old and attends second grade at highland creek elementary school where she is reportedly doing well academically sol was also evaluated for speech services as a toddler and was discharged after meeting all of her goals so the mother has some frame of reference for what therapy progress can look like mateo's mother lucía rodríguez flores works the night shift at compass fiber manufacturing and his father carlos flores mejía works during the week for green valley landscaping the family relies heavily on mateo's grandmother rosa mejía de flores who lives with them and provides most of the daytime childcare rosa speaks only spanish to mateo and reports that he understands her well but mostly responds in single words or gestures the family also has a dog named paz who mateo is very attached to and often tries to call by making an open mouth vowel sound that his mother interprets as an attempt at her name

language exposure at home is estimated at about 70 percent spanish and 30 percent english per parent report mateo was cared for primarily in spanish until he began attending little sprouts bilingual academy at 18 months of age where he is currently in a classroom with his teacher ms jennifer lopez and an assistant teacher mr david kim his teacher reports that he is affectionate and social with peers but is sometimes hard to understand and gets frustrated when peers do not know what he wants one classmate in particular named liam park is reported to often speak for mateo in group activities which the teacher feels may be reducing mateo's own spontaneous attempts to communicate the mother also shared that mateo's paternal aunt luz flores mejía who lives nearby and visits weekly often finishes his sentences for him when he gets stuck which has become a topic of gentle disagreement between her and the mother regarding how much support is helpful

mateo's father carlos flores mejía was born and raised in the village of la esperanza in the department of intibucá honduras near the family home at barrio el calvario and the family still has close relatives there including mateo's paternal grandfather the family visited for three weeks in the summer of 2024 during that trip mateo's exposure to spanish increased substantially per parent report and his father feels this trip helped his spanish vocabulary mateo's mother also reports a prior speech and language screening at 2 years 6 months of age through the cdsa initial intake which flagged concerns but did not meet criteria for immediate enrollment at that time and he was placed on a monitoring plan before full eligibility testing occurred the following year

early intervention and developmental services

mateo was found eligible for early intervention services through mecklenburg county children's developmental services agency with an ifsp dated december 2 2023 his current ifsp outcome outcome 2 addresses expressive language and ifsp outcome outcome 3 addresses speech sound intelligibility his service coordinator yesenia ortiz has conducted the required six month reviews with the most recent review completed on may 20 2026 he currently receives individual speech therapy through carolina bilingual speech therapy pllc with his treating clinician elena castillo and he also receives occupational therapy through a separate contracted agency with brittany sanders ot addressing fine motor and self feeding skills

current therapy and school schedule

day | start time | stop time | location
monday | 9:00 am | 9:45 am | carolina bilingual speech therapy pllc south park office
wednesday | 3:30 pm | 4:15 pm | little sprouts bilingual academy classroom on east boulevard
friday | 10:00 am | 10:45 am | flores family home 4821 old pineville road
every other tuesday | 1:00 pm | 1:30 pm | occupational therapy at south park office

assessment procedures and results

mateo was assessed using a combination of standardized and informal measures administered in both spanish and english with support from bilingual interpreter mariana flores no relation to the family who assisted with administration of parent interview items and cross checking of spanish responses billing for the evaluation session was submitted under cpt codes 92523 and 92522 mateo separated from his grandmother rosa mejía de flores easily and engaged readily with toys and picture materials he required frequent redirection to remain seated and his attention was judged to be age appropriate for the testing context

test | domain | standard score | percentile | age equivalent
preschool language scales fifth edition (pls-5) spanish | auditory comprehension | 78 | 7th percentile | 2;9
pls-5 spanish | expressive communication | 72 | 3rd percentile | 2;6
pls-5 english | auditory comprehension | 81 | 10th percentile | 3;0
pls-5 english | expressive communication | 75 | 5th percentile | 2;9
goldman fristoe test of articulation third edition (gfta-3) | sounds in words | 68 | 2nd percentile | 2;3

on the pls-5 spanish form mateo obtained an auditory comprehension standard score of 78 falling in the 7th percentile and an expressive communication standard score of 72 falling in the 3rd percentile with a confidence interval of 65-79 on the english form his auditory comprehension standard score was 81 at the 10th percentile and his expressive communication standard score was 75 at the 5th percentile with a confidence interval of 68-82 indicating a relative strength in english comprehension but delays present across both languages which supports a true language disorder rather than typical second language acquisition by comparison his screening scores at 2;6 on an informal checklist were reported as below the 10th percentile in both languages so his composite scores today reflect some gains since that time though he remains well below expectations

on the gfta-3 mateo scored 68 standard score falling at the 2nd percentile with an age equivalent of 2;3 he demonstrated consistent substitution of /k/ for /t/ and /g/ for /d/ a fronting pattern as well as final consonant deletion for example he produced "ba" for the target word "ball" and "ca" for the target word "cup" stimulability testing showed he could approximate [k] in isolation with moderate cues but not yet in words his intelligibility in connected speech was estimated at 40 percent to unfamiliar listeners and 65 percent to familiar listeners his mother lucía rodríguez flores reports that at home he is understood more easily by rosa mejía de flores than by his father carlos flores mejía who is away from home most of the week

informal language sampling showed mateo using primarily single words and occasional two word combinations such as "mas agua" and "no quiero" he demonstrated frequent word final consonant omissions coded as [EW] throughout the sample per salt coding conventions and required moderate cues to imitate three word models and maximal cues to imitate four word models his mean length of utterance was calculated at approximately 1.4 morphemes which falls well below expectations for a child his age in either language he produced roughly 3 of 5 trial targets correctly when given a visual and verbal model and about 8 of 10 single words correctly when naming familiar objects spontaneously

oral mechanism exam was within normal limits for structure and function with adequate range of motion of the articulators no concerns were noted for feeding or swallowing at this time and no drooling or oral motor weakness was observed mateo's weight and growth have been appropriate per his most recent pediatric visit on may 28 2026 with dr patricia nguyen a brief voice and fluency screening was also conducted and was unremarkable with no concerns for stuttering, vocal quality, or resonance noted by either parent or clinician

impressions

based on standardized testing parent and teacher report and informal observation mateo presents with a mixed receptive expressive language disorder affecting both spanish and english consistent with icd-10 code f80.2 mixed receptive expressive language disorder he also presents with a phonological disorder consistent with icd-10 code f80.0 phonological disorder his difficulties are not attributable to typical bilingual language development given that delays are documented across both of his languages rather than isolated to one he continues to meet criteria for ongoing speech and language services under his current ifsp through mecklenburg county children's developmental services agency his strengths include good social engagement, intact hearing, a supportive and motivated family, and a stable childcare arrangement with his grandmother rosa mejía de flores which should support consistent carryover of home strategies

recommendations

1 continue individual speech and language therapy twice weekly focusing on expressive vocabulary growth, two word combinations, and phonological awareness using a combination of hanen parent coaching strategies and the cycles phonological approach
2 incorporate prompt tactile cueing to support articulatory placement for fronted sounds
3 continue bilingual service delivery alternating spanish and english sessions to support both languages equally rather than favoring one
4 refer for a repeat audiological evaluation in six months given his history of recurrent otitis media and prior pe tube placement
5 provide parent training using hanen it takes two to talk strategies to increase responsive communication at home including with his grandmother rosa mejía de flores
6 continue close collaboration with little sprouts bilingual academy staff including ms jennifer lopez and mr david kim to support carryover of targets in the classroom and to reduce peer over-interpreting such as that described with liam park
7 encourage extended family members including luz flores mejía to use expectant pauses and wait time rather than finishing mateo's sentences for him
8 reassess in approximately six months to monitor progress and determine continued eligibility for services under his ifsp

summary and disposition

this report has been reviewed with the family and a copy has been forwarded to yesenia ortiz service coordinator at mecklenburg county children's developmental services agency and to dr patricia nguyen at atrium health pediatrics university city please direct any questions regarding this report to elena castillo m.s. ccc-slp at carolina bilingual speech therapy pllc she can be reached at 704-555-0199 or by email at elena.castillo@carolinabilingualslp.com additional information about services, scheduling, and insurance is available at www.carolinabilingualslp.com

Estimados Luis y Carolina,

Les escribo esta carta para compartir con ustedes los resultados de la evaluación de habla y lenguaje que le hicimos a su hija María José Castillo Fernández el 25 de septiembre de 2026 en nuestra oficina. Quiero explicarles todo con calma y en términos sencillos, porque sé que a veces estas evaluaciones pueden sonar muy técnicas. Si después de leer esta carta tienen preguntas, por favor llámenme o escríbanme; mi información de contacto está al final.

**Información del expediente**

Nombre de la niña: María José Castillo Fernández, a quien en casa llaman cariñosamente "Majo"
Fecha de nacimiento: 14 de marzo de 2022
Edad al momento de la evaluación: 4;6
Expediente clínico: BSP-2026-0547
Número de Medicaid: NC9284731B
Evaluadora: Marisol Vega, M.S., CCC-SLP
Agencia que autoriza el servicio: Centro de Servicios de Desarrollo Infantil del Condado de Wake (conocido como el CDSA del condado de Wake)
Coordinadora de servicios: Diane Walker

Yo trabajo como patóloga del habla y el lenguaje bilingüe para Bilingual Speech Pathways of the Triangle, PLLC, a la que muchas familias simplemente llaman Bilingual Speech Pathways, o por sus siglas, BSPT. Hice esta evaluación en nuestras oficinas en 4521 Falls of Neuse Road, Suite 210, Raleigh, NC 27609.

**Antecedentes**

María José fue referida a nuestra clínica por su pediatra, la Dra. Patricia Nguyen, del Triangle Kids Pediatrics – Campus de WakeMed North Healthplex, quien notó durante la revisión de los 4 años que el habla de Majo era difícil de entender, incluso para personas que la conocen bien. Ustedes también me contaron, durante nuestra primera llamada el 3 de agosto de 2026, que les preocupaba que María José mezclara sonidos al hablar tanto en español como en inglés, y que a veces se frustrara cuando sus maestras en la guardería no la entendían.

María José asiste actualmente a Sunny Days Early Learning Center, en el salón de niños de 4 años, de lunes a viernes de 7:30 a.m. a 5:00 p.m.. Su maestra principal, la señorita Heather Collins, me compartió por escrito que Majo es una niña alegre, sociable y curiosa, pero que a veces repite la misma palabra varias veces para que sus compañeros de clase le entiendan, y que juega mucho con su amiguita Sofía Reyes, con quien comparte mesa a la hora de comer. El próximo otoño, María José entrará a kínder en Hilltop Elementary School, la escuela que le corresponde por su dirección.

**Historia de nacimiento y médica**

Según el historial que ustedes compartieron y que confirmé con los registros médicos que nos autorizaron a revisar, María José nació el 14 de marzo de 2022 en el WakeMed Health & Hospitals, Campus de Raleigh, a las 36 semanas de gestación, con un peso de 6 libras 4 onzas. Recibió puntuaciones de Apgar de 7 y 8 al minuto y a los cinco minutos. Debido a que nació antes de tiempo y tuvo dificultad inicial para regular su temperatura, pasó 11 días en la unidad de cuidados intensivos neonatales del mismo WakeMed Health & Hospitals, Campus de Raleigh antes de poder ir a casa.

A los 18 meses, el otorrinolaringólogo Dr. Robert Hale, de UNC Health Rex Audiología Pediátrica, Campus de Rex, diagnosticó a María José con otitis media recurrente, y le colocaron tubos de ventilación bajo el código de procedimiento CPT 69436. La audióloga, Dra. Jennifer Suh, realizó una prueba de audición el 9 de febrero de 2024 en el mismo centro y encontró audición dentro de los límites normales en ambos oídos después de la cirugía. No hay antecedentes de hospitalizaciones adicionales, convulsiones ni problemas de visión. María José toma únicamente un multivitamínico diario y no tiene alergias conocidas.

El diagnóstico que estamos documentando hoy, bajo el código ICD-10 F80.2 (trastorno mixto del lenguaje receptivo-expresivo), junto con un segundo código, ICD-10 F80.0 (trastorno fonológico), refleja los hallazgos de esta evaluación, que explico más abajo.

**Historia familiar y de lenguaje**

María José vive en 1842 Birchwood Lane, Apex, NC 27502, con su mamá, Carolina Fernández Ibarra; su papá, Luis Castillo Medina; y su hermano mayor, Joaquín Castillo Fernández, de 8 años. Su abuela materna, Rosa Ibarra Soto, vive a pocas calles y cuida a María José y a Joaquín tres tardes por semana mientras su mamá, Carolina, trabaja en el turno vespertino en Blue Ridge Produce Distributors. También tienen una perrita llamada Luna, a quien María José menciona con frecuencia en nuestras sesiones.

Carolina nació y creció en el pueblo de El Rosario, en el departamento de Intibucá, Honduras, y llegó a Carolina del Norte hace once años. Luis nació en Raleigh, de padres mexicanos. En casa, los dos padres hablan principalmente español con los niños, aunque Joaquín, que ya está en segundo grado, a veces cambia al inglés sin que se lo pidan. Carolina me contó que ella habla con María José casi siempre en español, mientras que Luis alterna entre los dos idiomas según el tema de conversación. En la guardería, la señorita Heather Collins le habla a María José en inglés, así que la niña ha estado expuesta a los dos idiomas desde que nació.

Según el reporte de los padres, María José dijo sus primeras palabras alrededor de los 16 meses, más tarde de lo esperado, y empezó a combinar dos palabras cerca de los 30 meses. No hubo pérdida de habilidades del lenguaje ya adquiridas. Carolina y Luis describen a María José como una niña cariñosa, imaginativa y persistente, que disfruta jugar a la "cocinita" y dibujar, pero que se frustra y a veces llora cuando no logra que la entiendan, sobre todo con personas fuera de la familia inmediata.

No hay antecedentes familiares reportados de trastornos del habla o del lenguaje, aunque Luis mencionó que él mismo tuvo terapia de habla cuando era niño, por razones que no recuerda con claridad.

**Procedimientos de evaluación**

Realicé esta evaluación completamente en español, el idioma en el que María José se siente más cómoda y el que ustedes me indicaron que preferían para la sesión. Usé las siguientes pruebas e instrumentos:

- Preschool Language Scale-5 (PLS-5), edición en español, para medir comprensión y expresión del lenguaje.
- Goldman-Fristoe Test of Articulation-3 (GFTA-3), adaptado y administrado de forma informal con apoyo bilingüe, para evaluar la producción de sonidos.
- Muestra de lenguaje espontáneo grabada durante 20 minutos de juego libre.
- Observación clínica de la interacción social y el juego.
- Entrevista con los padres usando un cuestionario de desarrollo bilingüe.

También conversé por teléfono con la señorita Heather Collins el 15 de septiembre de 2026 para conocer cómo se comunica María José en el salón de clases.

**Resultados de las pruebas**

María José cooperó bien durante toda la sesión, aunque necesitó algunos descansos cortos y claves visuales para mantenerse enfocada. Sus resultados en el PLS-5 fueron los siguientes:

| Subprueba | Puntuación estándar | Percentil | Intervalo de confianza |
|---|---|---|---|
| Comprensión Auditiva | 82 | 12 | 73-83 |
| Comunicación Expresiva | 78 | 7 | 70-86 |
| Lenguaje Total | 79 | 8 | 72-85 |

Estas puntuaciones indican que tanto la comprensión como la expresión del lenguaje de María José están por debajo de lo esperado para su edad, con una debilidad algo mayor en el lenguaje expresivo. Su edad equivalente de lenguaje general fue de 3;2, comparado con su edad real de 4;6.

En cuanto a la articulación, con el GFTA-3 obtuvo una puntuación estándar de 75, en el percentil 5, con un intervalo de confianza de 68-82. Observé los siguientes patrones en su habla:

- Sustituye el sonido /ɾ/ por [w] en posición media, por ejemplo dice "pewo" en vez de "perro".
- Omite el sonido /s/ al final de las palabras, por ejemplo dice "do" en vez de "dos".
- Sustituye /k/ por /t/ en algunas palabras, como cuando dijo "tasa" en lugar de "casa".
- En inglés, mostró patrones parecidos; por ejemplo dijo "wabbit" en vez de "rabbit".

Durante la muestra de lenguaje espontáneo, María José produjo oraciones de entre 3 y 5 palabras, con errores frecuentes de concordancia de género y número en español (por ejemplo, dijo "la perro" en vez de "el perro"). Logró responder correctamente a preguntas de "qué" y "dónde" en 8 de 10 intentos, pero tuvo más dificultad con preguntas de "por qué", respondiendo correctamente solo en 3 de 5 intentos, incluso con claves de apoyo moderadas. Con claves mínimas logró imitar estructuras de oración más largas en 6 de 10 ensayos.

En el área social, María José mostró buen contacto visual, tomó turnos apropiadamente en el juego y buscó mi atención para compartir cosas que le interesaban, lo cual es una fortaleza importante.

**Impresiones clínicas**

Con base en estos resultados, en la información que ustedes y la señorita Heather Collins compartieron, y en mi observación directa, considero que María José presenta un trastorno mixto del lenguaje receptivo-expresivo (ICD-10 F80.2) junto con un trastorno fonológico (ICD-10 F80.0). Es importante que sepan que estos resultados no se deben a que María José esté aprendiendo dos idiomas al mismo tiempo. Las dificultades que observamos aparecen en ambos idiomas, lo cual nos indica que el problema está en el desarrollo del lenguaje en general, y no en el bilingüismo.

Las fortalezas de María José incluyen su deseo de comunicarse, su capacidad de jugar simbólicamente, su buena atención conjunta y su disposición para intentar repetir palabras cuando se le pide. Estas fortalezas son una base excelente para el progreso en terapia.

**Recomendaciones**

1. Recomiendo que María José reciba terapia de habla y lenguaje dos veces por semana, sesiones de 30 minutos, de manera individual, con un enfoque bilingüe. Nuestro equipo en Bilingual Speech Pathways of the Triangle, PLLC puede continuar brindando este servicio si así lo desean, o pueden solicitarlo a través del CDSA del condado de Wake con otro proveedor autorizado.
2. Sugiero que la terapia incluya un enfoque de tipo Cycles para los patrones de sonido que describí arriba, junto con estrategias de modelaje de lenguaje tipo Hanen para apoyar el crecimiento de oraciones más largas en casa.
3. Para la articulación, recomiendo trabajar primero en los sonidos /s/ y /k/, ya que estos afectan más la claridad de su habla, antes de abordar /ɾ/.
4. En casa, les sugiero seguir hablándole a María José en el idioma con el que se sientan más cómodos; no hay ninguna razón para dejar de usar el español. Pueden ayudarla repitiendo lo que dice de forma correcta, sin pedirle que lo repita ella misma, por ejemplo: si dice "tasa", pueden responder "sí, la casa es bonita".
5. Recomiendo una actualización del IFSP o la creación de un Plan de Educación Individualizado antes de que María José empiece en Hilltop Elementary School, para asegurar que los servicios continúen sin interrupción. La coordinadora de servicios, Diane Walker, del CDSA del condado de Wake, puede ayudarles con ese proceso; también pueden comunicarse con la oficina de WIC si necesitan apoyo adicional con recursos familiares.
6. Sugiero una reevaluación en 6 meses para medir el progreso, tentativamente alrededor de marzo de 2027.
7. Si en algún momento notan cambios en la audición de María José, como pedir que se repitan las cosas con frecuencia, recomiendo una nueva evaluación con la Dra. Jennifer Suh en UNC Health Rex Audiología Pediátrica, Campus de Rex.

**Próximos pasos**

Mi asistente administrativa se comunicará con ustedes esta semana para programar el horario regular de terapia. Si prefieren, pueden escribirme directamente a mvega@bilingualspeechpathways.com o llamar a nuestra oficina al (919) 555-0148. También pueden encontrar más información sobre nuestros servicios bilingües, incluyendo materiales educativos gratuitos para familias, en nuestro sitio web, www.bilingualspeechpathways.com.

Quiero agradecerles por la confianza que han puesto en nuestro equipo y por todo el esfuerzo que ya están haciendo en casa para apoyar a María José. Es una niña encantadora, y con el apoyo adecuado estoy segura de que hará un progreso maravilloso. No duden en contactarme si tienen cualquier pregunta sobre este reporte o sobre los próximos pasos.

Con cariño y respeto,

Marisol Vega, M.S., CCC-SLP
Patóloga del Habla y el Lenguaje
Bilingual Speech Pathways of the Triangle, PLLC (BSPT)
4521 Falls of Neuse Road, Suite 210, Raleigh, NC 27609

His mother, D.H., works full-time at Blue Ridge Linens and picks up weekend shifts at a second job; she could not attend today. O: Continued work on target sounds using PROMPT cueing and structured Cycles drill. Mateo produced /k/ in isolation with min cues 8/10 trials, improved from last session's 3 of 5. In word-final position he attempted the target word "cake," producing [keɪ] for "cake" with mod cues needed for closure.

Reviewed recent PLS-5 (readministered 09/22/2026) results with family: Auditory Comprehension standard score 78 (73-83 95% CI), Expressive Communication standard score 81 (76-86), Total Language Score 79, 9th percentile. Age equivalent for expressive language fell in the 2;6–3;0 range, consistent with Mateo's chronological age of 3;4.

text:
speech-language evaluation report

patient name: María José Hernández Gutiérrez
preferred name: Majo
date of birth: March 3, 2021
chronological age at evaluation: 5;7
date of evaluation: October 2, 2026
sessions: September 25, 2026 and October 2, 2026
medicaid id: 987654321B
case number: CDSA-2026-04821
primary language of home: Spanish and English
referral source: Dr. Patel, pediatrician, and service coordinator Carmen Ríos
evaluator: Jennifer Alvarez, MS CCC-SLP, bilingual speech-language pathologist, Piedmont Bilingual Therapy Associates
interpreter: Marta Lopez, Spanish language interpreter
contact phone: (336) 555-0148
contact email: lucia.hernandez88@mailbox.com
address: 4521 Hollyhock Lane, Greensboro, Guilford County, NC 27405

background and referral

majo was referred for a comprehensive speech and language evaluation by Dr. Patel after her nine month well child check where mom Lucía Hernández Castillo reported ongoing concerns about unclear speech and limited sentence use the referral was also prompted by the service coordinator Carmen Ríos who works through the Agencia de Coordinación de Servicios Infantiles del Condado de Guilford known locally as ACSI mom reports majo was already receiving some home visiting support but the family wanted a full bilingual evaluation before the upcoming ifsp review which the family understood would happen sometime around November 2026 the family was connected to the Centro de Servicios de Desarrollo Infantil del Piedmont commonly called the CDSA about eight months ago and that office has been coordinating majo's early intervention services since then

mom and dad Ricardo Gutiérrez Molina both attended today's session along with majo's older brother Diego who is nine and in fourth grade at Oak Hollow Elementary the baby sister Valentina who is eighteen months old stayed home with the grandmother Rosa Castillo who lives with the family and helps with childcare most weekdays mom reports the household also relies on a close family friend who sometimes watches the kids Esperanza Ramírez who the kids call tía esperanza even though she is not actually related

session one ran from 9:15 am to 10:45 am on September 25, 2026 and focused on parent interview case history review and informal observation session two ran from 1:30 pm to 3:00 pm on October 2, 2026 and included standardized testing and a language sample both sessions were conducted bilingually with the interpreter Marta Lopez present for portions of parent interview to support mom's preferred language dad is more comfortable in english and participated directly without interpretation

birth and medical history

mom reports pregnancy was mostly unremarkable though she had some bleeding early in the first trimester that resolved on its own majo was born at 38 weeks gestation via vaginal delivery at Moses Cone Women's Hospital birth weight was 6 lbs 4 oz apgar scores were 8 and 9 at one and five minutes mom denies nicu stay or complications after birth majo did have a brief hospitalization around June 2022 for a high fever that turned out to be a viral illness no lasting effects reported

developmental milestones were reported as generally on time for gross motor majo walked around 13 months fine motor also age appropriate per mom's report speech and language milestones were slower first words emerged closer to 20 months and were mostly single words in spanish mom reports majo did not combine words into short phrases until somewhere around 2;6 which is later than her older brother diego who mom says was talking in sentences by two

hearing was screened at birth and passed a more recent screening done through the pediatrician's office on August 14, 2026 also showed normal hearing bilaterally no history of chronic ear infections reported though mom recalls one or two episodes of otitis media around age two that resolved with antibiotics vision has not been formally screened outside of the pediatrician's routine exam no concerns noted there majo is not on any regular medications family history is notable for dad's brother who mom describes as "a late talker who eventually caught up and is fine now" no other family history of speech language or developmental concerns reported

current pediatric diagnosis on file includes a developmental language disorder code the pediatrician's note lists ICD-10 F80.1 and the clinic has previously billed evaluation services under CPT 92523 for combined speech and language evaluation

family and language history

the home language is predominantly spanish mom and dad both grew up speaking spanish mom Lucía was born and raised in the village of El Rosario in the department of Intibucá in Honduras and moved to the United States when she was nineteen dad Ricardo grew up in a small town called San Marcos also in Honduras and came to the US a few years before meeting mom they met here in Greensboro through mutual friends and have been together about eleven years

at home the family speaks spanish close to ninety percent of the time english is used more with diego's homework and some tv shows majo attends a bilingual daycare program called Little Learners Bilingual Daycare about four mornings a week where instruction is split roughly half spanish half english her main teacher there is Ms. Ortiz who mom says has been wonderful about flagging concerns and sending home notes majo's favorite friend at daycare is a little girl named Sofía who mom says majo talks about constantly even though her speech about sofía is sometimes hard to understand

mom reports no concerns about majo's hearing or understanding when spoken to in either language the concern is mainly in how clearly majo produces words and how long her sentences are compared to peers her age diego is reported to be fully bilingual with no speech or language concerns and functions as an unofficial translator for majo sometimes which mom says she tries to discourage because she wants majo to practice using her own words

the family's dog Luna is frequently mentioned by majo at home and was brought up spontaneously during the session when majo pointed to a picture of a dog in a book and said "luna" clearly

behavioral observations

majo presented as a friendly and social child throughout both sessions she separated easily from mom and engaged readily with the evaluator and the interpreter eye contact was consistently appropriate play skills were age appropriate majo engaged in both functional and some pretend play during unstructured portions of the session attention and engagement were adequate for testing though majo did show some frustration when asked to repeat items multiple times particularly on more structured language tasks

articulation and phonology

connected speech was moderately difficult to understand for an unfamiliar listener estimated intelligibility in connected speech was roughly 60% in spanish and 55% in english single word intelligibility was somewhat higher around 75% in both languages a number of sound substitutions and simplifications were noted across both languages consistent with a phonological delay rather than an isolated articulation disorder

in english majo produced /k/ as /t/ in word initial position for example saying "tat" for the target word "cat" final consonant deletion was also noted for example majo said "ca" for the target "cup" cluster reduction was observed in words like "spoon" which majo produced as "poon" liquid gliding was present with /ɹ/ frequently realized as [w] for example "wabbit" for the target "rabbit"

in spanish similar patterns were noted the trilled /r/ was consistently substituted with [l] for example majo said "losa" for the target word "rosa" the tapped /ɾ/ was also inconsistent in medial position for example "pedo" for the target "perro" cluster reduction appeared in spanish as well for example "flo" produced as "fo" for the target "flor"

stimulability testing showed that majo was able to produce /k/ correctly in isolation and in a few single word contexts with moderate cues suggesting some capacity for change with direct instruction final consonants were more difficult to elicit even with maximal cues which is consistent with the pattern of final consonant deletion being more entrenched

language sample and informal observation

a language sample was collected during both structured and unstructured play majo's mean length of utterance in words was calculated using salt conventions and came out to approximately 2.8 which falls below expectations for her age utterances were coded for completeness and several were marked with the exact word code [EW] where majo substituted or omitted a target word within an otherwise intelligible sentence

examples from the language sample in english include majo pointing to a toy and saying "i want it" which was a complete simple sentence and majo saying "dog run" when shown a picture book which omitted both the article and a verb marker in spanish majo said "quiero jugo" correctly when asking for juice but also produced "yo no sabe" which shows a subject verb agreement error that is somewhat beyond what would be expected for typical code switching alone

majo used a total of four different wh questions appropriately across both sessions mostly "qué" and "what" with occasional attempts at "dónde" she did not produce any complex sentences with subordinate clauses in either language during the sample which is below expectation for a child her age

standardized testing results

the following measures were administered across both languages where appropriate norms exist standard scores and percentile ranks are reported along with ninety five percent confidence intervals administration dates are included in the table because testing occurred across two separate sessions

| test / subtest | date administered | standard score | percentile rank | 95% CI |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| PLS-5 Spanish Auditory Comprehension | September 25, 2026 | 78 | 7th | 73-83 |
| PLS-5 Spanish Expressive Communication | September 25, 2026 | 72 | 3rd | 67-77 |
| PLS-5 English Auditory Comprehension | October 2, 2026 | 81 | 10th | 76-86 |
| PLS-5 English Expressive Communication | October 2, 2026 | 74 | 4th | 69-79 |
| Goldman-Fristoe 3 Sounds-in-Words | October 2, 2026 | 70 | 2nd | 64-76 |
| CELF Preschool-3 Core Language | October 2, 2026 | 76 | 5th | 71-81 |

age equivalent scores were also calculated for several measures majo's receptive language age equivalent fell around 3;9 and her expressive language age equivalent fell around 3;4 both of which represent a gap of close to 2 years from her chronological age of 5;7 the articulation age equivalent on the goldman fristoe fell around 3;6-3;11

nonverbal cognitive screening was not formally completed during this evaluation but informal observation during play and task engagement did not suggest a cognitive concern separate from the speech and language profile the service coordinator Carmen Ríos indicated that a separate developmental screening through the cdsa had already ruled out broader developmental delay outside of communication

oral mechanism exam

oral structures were within normal limits for strength range of motion and symmetry no concerns noted with the lips tongue jaw or palate diadochokinetic rates were mildly slower than expected for age but this is thought to be secondary to the phonological delay rather than a separate motor speech disorder no signs suggestive of apraxia were observed though continued monitoring is recommended given the combination of inconsistent sound errors and reduced intelligibility

summary and clinical impressions

based on parent report direct testing and language sample analysis majo presents with a moderate expressive and receptive language delay affecting both spanish and english along with a moderate phonological disorder that further reduces her overall intelligibility majo's language skills are weaker than expected in both of her languages which supports a true language disorder rather than a language difference related to typical bilingual development or typical second language acquisition this distinction matters because majo's deficits are present and roughly comparable across both languages rather than isolated to the less dominant one

the pattern of sound errors including final consonant deletion cluster reduction and liquid substitutions in both languages is consistent with a phonological delay that would be expected to respond to structured intervention majo's stimulability on several target sounds with moderate cues is a positive prognostic sign

majo's social communication and play skills are a relative strength and support a good foundation for intervention mom and dad are highly engaged and motivated which is also a strong protective factor the family's current connection to the CDSA and to service coordinator Carmen Ríos provides a good existing structure to build continued services around

recommendations

1 majo should continue to receive speech and language intervention through her existing ifsp with services increasing from the current frequency given the degree of delay identified today sessions twice weekly for thirty minutes each are recommended rather than the current once weekly schedule

2 intervention should address both languages rather than focusing on english alone given that majo's home language is primarily spanish and this is the language she will continue to need for communication with her family and community

3 phonological intervention should target cluster reduction and final consonant deletion first using a cycles approach given majo's stimulability on several sounds with moderate cues the Cycles approach is recommended as a starting point for structured phonological intervention

4 expressive language goals should target increasing mean length of utterance and improving use of grammatical morphemes in both languages a combination of modeling and expansion strategies consistent with Hanen style parent coaching is recommended to support carryover at home

5 continued collaboration with daycare staff including Ms. Ortiz is recommended to support consistent language exposure and early literacy activities in the classroom setting

6 a follow up hearing screening is not indicated at this time given the recent normal results from August 14, 2026 but should be repeated if any new ear infections occur

7 given mild concerns about diadochokinetic rate continued monitoring for signs of motor speech involvement is recommended if progress in therapy is slower than expected a referral for a more targeted motor speech evaluation should be considered at that point

8 the family should continue working with service coordinator Carmen Ríos through ACSI and the CDSA to update the ifsp to reflect these recommendations before the upcoming review currently anticipated for November 2026

9 parent training materials in spanish are recommended given mom's preference for spanish and her primary role in daily communication with majo

10 reassessment is recommended in approximately six months to monitor progress toward ifsp outcome IFSP Outcome 2 and IFSP Outcome 3 which address expressive language and intelligibility respectively

REVIEW DATES

- Next scheduled review: 03/29/2027

FAMILY CONCERNS AND PRIORITIES (in the family's own words)

- "Teo no nos dice lo que quiere, solo llora y señala" — Lucía reports that Mateo does not use words to ask for things and instead cries and points.
- "Queremos que hable español y inglés, no solo uno" — Héctor shared that the family wants Teo to develop both Spanish and English, since the home is Spanish-dominant but his older sister speaks English at school.
- Lucía stated, "Me preocupa que no juega con los otros niños en la guardería" — she is concerned Mateo does not play with peers at daycare.
- The family would like strategies they can use during mealtimes and bath time, since those are the times Mateo gets most frustrated.
- Héctor asked whether Mateo's stuttering-like repetitions are typical or a concern; team clarified these appear to be normal disfluencies at this stage.

FAMILY ROUTINES AND DAILY SCHEDULE

- 6:45 AM: Wakes up, nurses briefly with Lucía, then plays with his older sister Camila before breakfast
- 7:30 AM: Breakfast at home; family reports this is a good time for requesting more food with gestures
- 8:15 AM: Héctor drops Mateo and Camila at Little Acorn Treehouse on his way to work
- 8:30 AM–3:00 PM: Daycare day in Ms. Delgado's toddler room
- 3:15 PM: Pickup, usually by grandmother Rosa Fernández
- 4:00 PM: Outdoor play with neighbor child Noah; family notes Mateo mostly plays alongside Noah rather than with him
- 6:00 PM: Dinner; family uses this time to model simple words like "más" and "agua"
- 7:00 PM: Bath time, a favorite activity; Mateo babbles and sometimes imitates "agua" during splashing
- 7:45 PM: Books and bedtime routine with Lucía, often in Spanish

CHILD'S HEALTH AND DEVELOPMENTAL HISTORY

- Birth history: full-term, 39 weeks gestation, birth weight 7 lbs 4 oz, Apgar 8/9
- No significant hospitalizations; one ER visit for a febrile illness at 11 months
- Hearing screening passed bilaterally at birth and again at 02/2026
- Pediatric exam notes age-appropriate gross motor and fine motor skills; speech-language is the only area of concern

CURRENT SERVICE PROVIDERS AND OTHER AGENCIES

- Wake County Smart Start provided a referral for the family to Little Acorn Treehouse and continues to monitor quality
- Wake County WIC office supports nutrition; contact 919-555-3310
- Wake County DSS is not currently involved with the family
- Early intervention speech-language therapy through Carolina Pediatric Therapy Partners, billed under CPT code 92507
- Occupational therapy consult requested but not yet started; waiting on authorization
- Family also attends a Spanish-speaking parent support group facilitated by El Pueblo Family Resource Center

PRESENT LEVELS OF DEVELOPMENT

Communication

- Standardized assessment: Preschool Language Scales, Fifth Edition (PLS-5) Spanish
- Auditory Comprehension standard score: 76 (5th percentile)
- Expressive Communication standard score: 71 (3rd percentile)
- Total Language Score: 73, confidence interval 68-78
- Age equivalent for expressive language: 11-13 months
- Chronological age at testing: 2;4
- Expressive vocabulary estimated at 8-10 words across both languages, primarily in Spanish: "mamá," "papá," "agua," "más," "no"
- Receptive vocabulary stronger; follows 1-step directions 4 of 5 trials in Spanish and 2 of 5 in English
- Babbling is varied; uses jargon with intonation patterns resembling sentences
- No consistent word combinations observed
- Imitates target word "pelota" with moderate cues, producing [pe.ta]
- During the session, Mateo pointed to the ball and said "ba" approximating "pelota"

Speech Sound Production

- Limited consonant inventory: /m/, /p/, /b/, /n/ observed in babbling and single words
- No evidence of /k/ or /g/ at this time
- Oral mechanism exam within normal limits; no concerns for structure or function
- Feeding and swallowing not currently a concern per parent report

Social Communication and Play

- Joint attention emerging but inconsistent; follows a point about 50% of trials
- Does not yet use pointing to request
- Limited symbolic play observed; mostly exploratory/sensory play with toys
- At daycare, teacher Ms. Lopez (floater in Ms. Lopez's room during Mateo's nap transition week) reported Mateo watches peers but rarely initiates interaction
- Classroom peer Ava has started bringing Mateo toys, which he accepts but does not reciprocate verbally

ELIGIBILITY

- Mateo continues to meet eligibility for NC ITP services under the established developmental delay category in communication, per PLS-5 scores above
- ICD-10 code: F80.9 (Developmental disorder of speech and language, unspecified)

IFSP OUTCOMES, STRATEGIES, AND SERVICES

Outcome 1: Mateo will use 25 different words or signs across settings (home, daycare) to request, label, and comment, in Spanish and/or English.

- Strategies:
  - Family will model target words during daily routines (mealtime, bath time) using Hanen "It Takes Two to Talk" strategies, especially OWL (Observe, Wait, Listen)
  - SLP will use PROMPT tactile-kinesthetic cueing to support bilabial and nasal sound production
  - Daycare staff in Ms. Delgado's room will incorporate visual supports modeled after PECS during snack time to encourage requesting
  - Family will narrate actions in both Spanish and English without requiring repetition from Mateo

Outcome 2: Mateo will initiate joint attention and simple requests with familiar adults and peers during play, 4 of 5 opportunities, across two consecutive sessions.

- Strategies:
  - SLP will use Hanen strategies to follow Mateo's lead and expand on his communicative attempts
  - Family and grandmother Rosa Fernández will practice "wait time" of at least 5 seconds before offering a model
  - Introduce structured turn-taking games with peer Noah during outdoor play, using simple scripted phrases

Outcome 3: Mateo will increase his consonant inventory to include /t/, /d/, and /k/ in imitated and spontaneous words, measured by percentage of consonants correct.

- Strategies:
  - Cycles approach to target phonological patterns, cycling through final consonant deletion and velar fronting
  - Home practice list of target words sent weekly in Spanish, reviewed with family during sessions
  - SLP will track progress using percentage of consonants correct (PCC) at each session

Outcome 4: Family will report increased confidence supporting bilingual communication development at home.

- Strategies:
  - SLP will coach family on code-mixing being a typical and healthy part of bilingual development
  - Provide family with a bilingual vocabulary checklist to track new words at home
  - Discuss Kaufman Speech to Language Protocol hierarchy as a backup approach if motor planning concerns emerge

SERVICE DELIVERY
